As of the [[2010 United States census]],<ref name="GR2">{{cite web|url=https://factfinder.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/DEC/10_DP/DPDP1/0600000US2501330840?slice=GEO~0600000US2501330840|publisher=[[United States Census Bureau]]|access-date=January 12, 2020|title=Profile of General Population and Housing Characteristics: 2010 Demographic Profile Data - Holyoke city, Hampden County, Massachusetts|archive-url=https://archive.today/20200214060804/https://factfinder.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/DEC/10_DP/DPDP1/0600000US2501330840?slice=GEO~0600000US2501330840|archive-date=February 14, 2020|url-status=dead}}</ref> there were '''39,880 people''', 15,361 households, and 9,329 families residing in the city of [[Holyoke]], [[Massachusetts]]. The [[population density]] was 723.6/km{{sup|2}} (1,874/mi²). There were 16,384 housing units at an average density of 277.2/km{{sup|2}} (718.6/mi²).

The City of Holyoke has in its history, had a uniquely varied demography for its small population size. In the prime of the [[Second Industrial Revolution]], native-born residents ranged between 18 and 38 percent, as successive waves of Colombian, Dominican,  English, French-Canadian, Irish, German, Greek, Italian, Polish, Russian, Puerto Rican, Scottish and many other groups emigrated to Holyoke throughout the city's first century.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Immigration, Occupation and Inequality in Emergent Nineteenth-Century New England Cities|author1=Susan Hautaniemi Leonard|author2=Christopher Robinson|author3=Douglas L. Anderton|journal=Social Science History|date=Winter 2017|volume=XLI|issue=4|pages=645–671|pmc=5751957|pmid=29307945|doi=10.1017/ssh.2017.26}}</ref>

Despite being a small city, only reaching a peak estimated population of 65,286 estimated in 1916, Holyoke had a unique demography among cities in the United States, having the 3rd highest foreign born population in the 1890 census,<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0VAzAQAAMAAJ&pg=PR92-IA3|page=xciii|title=Report on Population of the United States at the Eleventh Census: 1890|volume=I|year=1895|publisher=Government Printing Office (GPO)|location=Washington, D.C.|isbn=9780883544464}}</ref> due to its syncretic culture industrial laborers. The proportion of immigrant residents was described in 1902 by journalist for the ''[[New-York Tribune]]'' as unequaled, noting "no other city in the country has so large a foreign population in comparison to its size", as the community made early efforts to both accommodate such numerous cultures, while fostering a sense of [[cultural assimilation]], and [[Americanization (immigration)|Americanization]].<ref name="AmericanizationNYTrib">{{cite news|title=The People of Holyoke; Great Proportion of Them Foreigners; What is Being Done for Their Americanization—Forces of Law, Education and Example|url=https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/lccn/sn83030214/1902-11-09/ed-1/seq-28/|work=New-York Tribune|date=November 9, 1902|page=14|location=New York|via=Chronicling America, Library of Congress}}</ref>

==Income==
For the period 2013–17, the estimated median annual income for a household in the city was $37,954, and the median income for a family was $46,940. Male full-time workers had a median income of $46,888 versus $41,406 for females. The [[per capita income]] for the city was $22,625. About 24.7% of families and 28.6% of the population were below the [[poverty line]], including 45.6% of those under age 18 and 19.8% of those age 65 or over.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://factfinder.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/ACS/17_5YR/DP03/1600000US2530840 |title=Selected Economic Characteristics: 2013–2017 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates (DP03): Holyoke city, Massachusetts |publisher=U.S. Census Bureau |work=American Factfinder |access-date=April 21, 2019 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20200213091844/https://factfinder.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/ACS/17_5YR/DP03/1600000US2530840 |archive-date=February 13, 2020 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

As of 2017, the city had the most recipients of [[Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program|Supplemental Nutrition Assistance]] per capita of any in Massachusetts, with 37% of residents receiving such benefits. Of all ZIP codes in the Commonwealth, including those of Boston, Holyoke had the third highest total households receiving such assistance, with the highest per capita of any of the state's 351 municipalities, representing 54% of all households.<ref>{{cite report|title=Revised Statewide ZIP Assistance Units and Recipients|date=June 20, 2017|publisher=Massachusetts Executive Office of Health and Human Services|url=https://www.mass.gov/eohhs/docs/dta/revised-statewide-zip-62017.xls|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170802120134/http://www.mass.gov/eohhs/docs/dta/revised-statewide-zip-62017.xls|archive-date=August 2, 2017}}
* {{cite web|url=https://factfinder.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/PEP/2017/PEPANNRES/0400000US25.06100|title=Annual Estimates of the Resident Population: April 1, 2010 to July 1, 2017; for all Minor Civil Divisions, Massachusetts]|publisher=US Census|access-date=August 14, 2019|archive-url=https://archive.today/20200213183043/https://factfinder.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/PEP/2017/PEPANNRES/0400000US25.06100|archive-date=February 13, 2020|url-status=dead}}
* {{cite web|url=https://factfinder.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/ACS/17_5YR/DP02/0400000US25.06000|title=SELECTED SOCIAL CHARACTERISTICS IN THE UNITED STATES [ACS_17_5YR_DP02]; for all Minor Civil Divisions, Massachusetts]|publisher=US Census|access-date=August 14, 2019|archive-url=https://archive.today/20200213114757/https://factfinder.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/ACS/17_5YR/DP02/0400000US25.06000|archive-date=February 13, 2020|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Measuring Inclusion in Small New England Cities|last1=Stacy|last2=Meixell|first1=Christina|first2=Brady|archive-date=January 28, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200128131901/https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/publication/101604/measuring_inclusion_in_small_new_england_cities_1.pdf|url=https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/publication/101604/measuring_inclusion_in_small_new_england_cities_1.pdf|publisher=Urban Institute}}</ref> A 2020 study by the [[Urban Institute]] found Holyoke to be the least socioeconomically inclusive city in New England for minorities, despite them representing the largest group demographically. The report found between 2010 and 2015 the racial educational attainment gap narrowed by 30%, however homeownership declined slightly, and the proportion of [[working poor]] marginally increased.<ref>{{cite news|title=Measuring Inclusion in Small New England Cities|last1=Stacy|last2=Meixell|first1=Christina|first2=Brady|archive-date=January 28, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200128131901/https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/publication/101604/measuring_inclusion_in_small_new_england_cities_1.pdf|url=https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/publication/101604/measuring_inclusion_in_small_new_england_cities_1.pdf|publisher=Urban Institute}}</ref>

==Precolonial settlement==
{{further|History of Springfield, Massachusetts#17th century}}
In the area around Holyoke and South Hadley Falls there were a number of tribes of native tribes, all belonging to the [[Algonquian peoples]]. Though records are sparse and incomplete, the area was settled by the [[Pocomtuc]], sometimes referred to as the [[Agawam people|Agawam]] or Nonotuck.<ref>{{cite web|archive-date=September 23, 2018|title=First Peoples- Overview|website=Our Plural History, Springfield, MA|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180923173833/http://ourpluralhistory.stcc.edu/firstpeoples/overview.html|url=http://ourpluralhistory.stcc.edu/firstpeoples/overview.html|publisher=Springfield Technical Community College|year=2009}}</ref> Little remains marking the legacy of the Connecticut Valley's indigenous population in Holyoke. One of the few notable examples was found during an early excavation for [[Holyoke Canal System|the canal system]] in 1847, when four skeletons were found by workmen in a makeshift tomb, all in the sitting position, facing eastward, with a mortar and pestle beside them, and a hollowed out underground chamber surrounding them.<ref>{{cite news|title=Indian Skeletons|date=December 17, 1847|page=2|work=Springfield Republican|location=Springfield, Mass.|quote=A correspondent at Ireland Depot Village (the new city) informs us that the workmen in excavating for the Canal there, yesterday, discovered the skeletons of four Indians, in a sitting posture, with their faces towards the East. Beside them were found a Mortar and Pestle of stone, such as were used by the Indians in pounding corn. What was quite as singular as any thing was, that a subterranean channel ran completely around the skeletons.}}</ref> A number of burial sites would also be unearthed during the development of [[The Flats, Holyoke, Massachusetts|Depot Hill]], and for a time DeRoy Park was known as [[Canonchet]] Park, as at least one such grave was found there. Other sites were discovered across the river where Bachelor Brook met the Connecticut, and in the early 20th century those who discovered those sites posited that artifacts might exist on the shores by [[Highland Park, Holyoke, Massachusetts|Highland Park]]. Ultimately the presence of the tribes to the west of [[Springfield, Massachusetts|Springfield]] and [[Hadley, Massachusetts|Hadley]] would keep many of the earliest pioneers from permanently settling in the 17th century.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Conant|first1=Howard | last2=Harper | first2=Wyatt E. | title=Complete program of Holyoke's seventy-fifth anniversary and home coming days : with a history of the city | year=1948 | oclc= 9694660 |url = https://archive.org/stream/completeprogramo00unse/#page/n0/mode/2up|page=8}}</ref>

In the early 20th century, many Amerindian artifacts were uncovered and exhibited by local architect W. J. Howes, who would lead lectures on tribe archaeology at the Holyoke Scientific Association and was a recipient of many gifts of pottery and arrowheads found by people in the valley.<ref>{{cite news|title=Indian Relics About Holyoke; Delved in Local Graves, Paper Read at Meeting of the Holyoke Scientific Association—Municipal and Political Matters|date=October 6, 1901|page=11|location=Springfield, Mass.|work=Springfield Republican}}
* {{cite news|title=Indian Relics May Be Found Through Holyoke Estates; Section Was Heart of Redskin Country—Tribe Feuds Recalled|page=11|work=Springfield Republican|location=Springfield, Mass.|date=April 1, 1928}}</ref>

==Ethnography==
[[File:Holyoke Immigration (1855-1920).svg|left|thumb|270px|Populations of first generation foreign-born nationals residing in Holyoke during the [[Second Industrial Revolution]]]]
[[File:Workers laying the last stone in the Holyoke Dam (1900).jpg|thumb|right|Workers standing beside the last stone laid in the [[Holyoke Dam]], January 5, 1900]]

Holyoke had witnessed such staggering growth from its founding until about 1900, that by 1902 the ''[[New-York Tribune]]'' reported the city contained 80% either first or second-generation immigrants, claiming that when adding the latter, no other city in the United States had as many residents per capita of foreign origin. At the time of writing, early efforts of [[Americanization (immigration)|Americanization]] had begun, with the city being described both by the ''Tribune'' and the Commonwealth's offices as being at the forefront of teaching immigrant groups English as a second language, as well as history, and civics. The groups involved in these efforts to foster a common Holyoke community amongst the different ethnic groups included private companies like [[William Skinner and Sons|William Skinner & Sons]], with the Skinners introducing the Skinner Coffeehouse meeting hall that year, as well as the local [[YMCA]], the Chamber of Commerce, and [[Holyoke Public Schools]], all providing classes, events, and other social gathering opportunities.<ref name="nytrib">{{cite news|title=Holyoke is Wrestling Successfully with One of the Greatest Problems Confronting this Nation; The People of Holyoke; Great Proportion of them Foreigners; What is Being Done for Their Americanization—Forces of Law, Education, and Example|page=14|work=New-York Tribune|location=New York|via=Library of Congress|date=November 9, 1902|url=https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/lccn/sn83030214/1902-11-09/ed-1/seq-28/}}</ref><ref name="educommonwealth">{{cite journal|journal=Division of University Extension, Americanization Bulletin of the Massachusetts Board of Education|volume=V|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VtsXAQAAIAAJ&pg=RA2-PA46|title=Paper of Miss Jennie E. Scolley|pages=46–48|date=January 1920|issue=1|location=Boston, Mass.}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|journal=Municipal Register of the City of Holyoke|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JMVEAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA200|title=Americanization|pages=200–201|year=1923|publisher=Dillon Printing & Publishing Company|location=Holyoke, Mass.}}</ref><ref name="educommonwealth2">{{cite journal|journal=Division of University Extension, Class and Correspondence Instruction Bulletin of the Massachusetts Board of Education|volume=VI|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gdsXAQAAIAAJ&pg=RA3-PA11|title=Significant Achievements and Activities in Massachusetts Communities|page=11|date=January 1921|issue=1|location=Boston, Mass.}}</ref>

Even as the [[Second Industrial Revolution]] drew to a close, the successive waves of immigration to the city seeking jobs and inexpensive housing continued. Originally settled by Yankee English, [[Irish Protestants]] and a few freemen, the first wave of immigration was largely [[Irish Catholics]] with a smaller demographic of [[Scottish people|Scots]], followed by waves [[French people|French]] and French-Canadians, then [[English people|English]] and [[English Canadians]], [[German people|Germans]], [[Italian people|Italians]], [[Polish people|Poles]], [[Jews]], and smaller groups of [[Han Chinese|Chinese]] and [[Greek people|Greeks]]. From the mid-20th century onward came a large wave of [[Puerto Ricans|Puerto Rican]] denizens, and by the end of the 20th century smaller groups of [[Colombians]], [[People of the Dominican Republic|Dominicans]], and [[Mexicans]] had settled in the city.<ref>{{cite book | last1=Green | first1=Constance McLaughlin |author-link=Constance McLaughlin Green|url=https://archive.org/stream/in.ernet.dli.2015.59808/2015.59808.Holyoke-Massachusetts-A-Case-History-Of-The-Inkistrial-Revolution-In-America#page/n11/mode/2up|title=Holyoke, Massachusetts; a case history of the industrial revolution in America | year=1939 | publisher=Yale University Press |location = New Haven |series=Yale Historical Publications|number=XXXIV|page=367}}</ref><ref name="Sears 2015">{{cite book|title=Legendary Locals of Holyoke|last=Sears|first=Jacqueline|pages=42, 66|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UfHBCQAAQBAJ|publisher=Arcadia Publishing|year=2015|isbn=9781439650783}}</ref> Because of these large immigration movements throughout the decades, as well as changes in American culture at large, and the many [[Holyoke, Massachusetts#Culture|contributions of Holyoke to American culture]] such as [[volleyball]], Holyoke has throughout its history had a varying [[melting pot|syncretic culture]] as the result of disparate groups and traditions.

===African-Americans===
[[File:Deacons of Bethlehem Baptist Church in 1973 (Holyoke, Mass).jpg|left|thumb|Deacons of Bethlehem Baptist Church, 1973, (''left to right'') Mansfield Stuckey, Willis C. Wilson, Harold Patton, Larry Rucks]]
[[File:Hermanns_Soehne_Association_Hall_(Dr_Mother_Elouise_Franklin_Church),_Holyoke,_Massachusetts.jpg|thumb|right|The Mother Elouise Franklin Church today, in [[South Holyoke]]; originally used as the meeting hall of the Sons of Hermann, it was renovated by the parishioners in 1973, an early example of reuse and revitalization in South Holyoke]]
As of 2010, there were 1,867 African-American or black residents living in Holyoke, and an estimated 11,539 according to the 2017 [[American Community Survey]].<ref name="Race2010">{{Cite web| url=https://factfinder.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/DEC/10_SF1/PCT23/0600000US2501330840| title=RACE - Universe: Total population, 2010 Census Summary File 1| publisher=U.S. Census Bureau American FactFinder| access-date=January 2, 2019| archive-url=https://archive.today/20200213233756/https://factfinder.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/DEC/10_SF1/PCT23/0600000US2501330840| archive-date=February 13, 2020| url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="2017Race">{{cite web|url=https://factfinder.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/ACS/17_5YR/B02001/0600000US2501330840|archive-url=https://archive.today/20200213235910/https://factfinder.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/ACS/17_5YR/B02001/0600000US2501330840|url-status=dead|archive-date=February 13, 2020|publisher=[[United States Census Bureau]]|access-date=January 12, 2020|title=Race: 2013-2017 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates - Holyoke city, Hampden County, Massachusetts}}</ref> Black families have resided in Holyoke since its days as Ireland Parish, with one of the earliest records being the marriage of Bushman Fuller and his bride Miss Flora Parry, on February 7, 1778.<ref>{{cite book|title=The New England Historical and Genealogical Register|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NNIb9Qf7k4kC&pg=PA58|publisher=New England Historic Genealogical Society|volume=XXIX|date=January 1875|page=58|isbn = 9780788401954}}</ref> Fuller, a freeman who had previously been a slave to one Joseph Ely of West Springfield, purchased his wife's freedom for $100 at the time, or $1 per bushel of wheat. The two would become part of a small but active black community that resided to the west of what is today called [[Elmwood, Holyoke, Massachusetts|Elmwood]] in modern-day the Jarvis Avenue/Homestead Avenue neighborhoods. When the Congregationalists joined the Baptists in the Baptist Village meetinghouse, according to an 1890 account of the city's church history, members of the black community "were cordially received and were treated with great kindness by both the pastor and people". Though segregated, a section of the pews was set aside for them at the front rows by the pulpit, in the southwest section of the sanctuary. Flora Fuller would go on become a prominent member of the Baptist Village community, serving as a [[History of medicine in the United States#Women|village nurse]] to its earliest residents, providing aid to the sick.<ref name="MD"/> Flora Fuller's daughter, Clorilla, would marry a William Jarvis, of the family for whom Jarvis Avenue is so-named.<ref name="reprint">{{cite news|title=The Black Community in Holyoke, 1770s-1970s|via=The Republican|location=Springfield, Mass.|last=DiCarlo|first=Ella M.|page=E01|date=February 22, 2007}}</ref>

The community remained relatively small but other families would arrive to the city after its founding as Holyoke, seeking work in the mills and factories there.<ref name="reprint"/> By 1926 a survey of churchgoers showed 67 black Protestant parishioners, and an [[African Methodist Episcopal Church]] had opened in [[The Flats, Holyoke, Massachusetts|The Flats]]. This church, affiliated with a counterpart in Springfield, would be defunct before World War II.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/ProtestantAndCatholicReligiousAndSocialInteractionInAnIndustrialCommunity-KennethWilsonUnderwood/page/n1|title=Protestant and Catholic: Religious And Social Interaction In An Industrial Community|last=Underwood|first=Kenneth Wilson|publisher=The Beacon Press|location=Beacon Hill, Boston|year=1957|oclc=1021289508}}</ref> In 1957, the New Hope [[Church of God in Christ]] parish was established under the leadership of Bishop C. W. Franklin and his wife Mother Elouise Franklin. Moving from a storefront to a permanent home in the former Hermannshalle in 1973, the church remains extant in South Holyoke today, christened as the Mother Elouise Franklin Church.<ref name="storyof">{{cite book | last1=Harper | first1=Wyatt E. | title=The Story of Holyoke | year=1973 | publisher=Centennial Committee of the City of Holyoke | oclc=8060402 |url = https://archive.org/stream/storyofholyoke00harp#page/n0/mode/2up}}</ref> For several years the black Bethlehem Baptist Church had been meeting in the old Lutheran Church building in South Holyoke after the Lutheran move to their current church on Northampton Street in 1955. Over the next several years the Baptist Church would take part in dialogue with the Greater Holyoke Council of Churches, as part of a survey and broader panel for public discussion of the issues facing black Holyoke families.<ref>{{cite book  |year=1962 |last=Smith|first=Bulkeley|title=Holyoke's Negro Families; report to the Greater Holyoke Council of Churches of a survey |publisher=Greater Holyoke Council of Churches |oclc= 22333856 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Homes, Jobs Top Problems for Negroes; Church Panel Reports Housing Substandard, Work Service|page=40|date=March 25, 1961|location=Springfield, Mass.}}</ref> In 1961 the city's public schools would accept 3 black students, along with 6 others attending Springfield and West Springfield, after [[Prince Edward County, Virginia]] closed its public schools to avoid implementing [[Desegregation in the United States|court-mandated integration]]. This action led to 1,700 black children being unable to attend private white schools and through a nationwide effort by the [[American Friends Service Committee]], working with the local Greater Holyoke Council of Churches, funds were raised for the schooling of these additional three pupils at [[Holyoke Public Schools]].<ref name="dicarlo"/><ref>{{cite news|title=American Friends' Worker Speaks Here Wednesday; Miss Jean Fairfax Will Discuss Desegregation Problems in Prince Edward County|date=October 8, 1961|location=Springfield, Mass.|work=Springfield Republican}}</ref> When the Reformed Church on Sargeant Street merged with the other Congregational churches in 1963, their former building, also previously used by German immigrants, became the home of the Bethlehem Baptist Church, which resides there today.<ref name="dicarlo">{{cite book |last=DiCarlo|first=Ella Merkel| title=Holyoke–Chicopee, a Perspective; 1882–1982 | year=1982 | publisher=[[Holyoke Transcript-Telegram|Transcript-Telegram Co.]] | oclc= 9299261|pages=366–368}}</ref>

{{external media | width = 210px | float = left |
| audio1 = [https://archive.org/details/occupytheairwaveshistoryofblackholyoke10.13.2019 ''History Of Black Holyoke'', with Erica Slocumb], October 13, 2019, on ''Occupy the Airwaves'' of [[WXOJ-LP]]}}
The 1960 US Census would record 148 black households, representing in total about 1% or about 500 individuals of the 52,689 population at that time. Within a decade two of the school district's own native sons went on to become household names. The first, Jim Jennings, would go on from [[Holyoke High School]] to play for [[Rutgers University]] as a [[running back]] in the early 1970s.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1973/09/09/archives/rutgers-eleven-to-key-its-offense-on-jennings-wagner-rated-strong.html|work=The New York Times|date=September 9, 1973|last=White|first=Gordon S. (Jr.)|title=Rutgers Eleven to Key Its Offense on Jennings; Wagner Rated Strong|page=224}}</ref> The other, [[Kenny Gamble (American football)|Kenny Gamble]] would go on from being a running back for [[Colgate University]] to being the inaugural recipient of the [[Walter Payton Award]], playing for the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] thereafter for four seasons. Gamble would later be inducted into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 2002.<ref>{{cite news|website=College Football Hall of Fame|publisher=National Football Foundation|url=https://footballfoundation.org/hof_search.aspx?hof=2063|title=Kenny Gamble|year=2002}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nfl.com/player/kennygamble/2500749/careerstats|title=Kenny Gamble|publisher=National Football League (NFL)}}</ref>

In 1983, after discussion between Mayor Proulx and the [[NAACP]], the City agreed to set up a Minority Action Committee, including the city's affirmative action officer, Victor Douglas, and the NAACP-appointed Louis Owens, an electrician and outspoken candidate for city council, who agreed with the mission of the body as a means to lobby for improved housing and economic opportunities for the city's black and Hispanic community.<ref>{{cite news|title=Candidate Owens backs action group|last=Moriarty|first=Jo-Ann|work=Springfield Union|location=Springfield, Mass.|page=2|date=August 15, 1983}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Mayor, NAACP agree — to a point|last=Moriarty|first=Jo-Ann|work=Springfield Union|location=Springfield, Mass.|page=3|date=August 12, 1983}}</ref>

In 2018 a doctoral candidate in [[UMass Amherst]]'s Afro-American Studies Department, Erika Slocumb, began documenting and archiving accounts of black Holyoke history, with support from the [[Wistariahurst Museum]] and funding by [[Mass Humanities]].<ref>{{cite web|archive-date=June 20, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190620132627/https://wistariahurst.org/black-holyoke-project-april-update/|url=https://wistariahurst.org/black-holyoke-project-april-update/|title=Black Holyoke Project: April Update|author=Erika Slocumb|date=23 April 2019 |publisher=Wistariahurst Museum}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|archive-date=June 20, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190620132815/https://wistariahurst.org/black-holyoke-uncovering-the-history-of-the-black-community-in-the-paper-city/|url=https://wistariahurst.org/black-holyoke-uncovering-the-history-of-the-black-community-in-the-paper-city/|title=Black Holyoke: Uncovering the History of the Black Community in the Paper City|publisher=Wistariahurst|date=January 26, 2018|author=Erika Slocumb}}</ref> Slocumb's work, ''Reliquary of Blackness: Documenting Black History in Holyoke'' was among those selected to be featured in the [[National Council on Public History]]'s 2020 national conference.<ref>{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200104191213/https://ncph.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/2020-Preliminary-Annual-Meeting-Program-for-web.pdf|url=https://ncph.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/2020-Preliminary-Annual-Meeting-Program-for-web.pdf|date=November 2019|archive-date=January 4, 2020|title='Threads of Change'; Annual Meeting of the National Council on Public History, March 18-21, 2020, Atlanta Georgia|publisher=National Council on Public History (NCPH)}}</ref>

Though [[African Americans#Terminology dispute|not necessarily identified with the handle African-American]], generally used to refer to the descendants of former enslaved black peoples, additionally in single-ancestry responses in 2017, 323 people identified as Subsaharan Africans, including 100 Zimbabweans, 93 Liberians, and 44 Kenyans, and 148 as non-Hispanic West Indians, including 88 Jamaicans and 44 Haitians.<ref name="SingleAncestry2017ACS">{{cite web|url=https://factfinder.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/ACS/17_5YR/B04004/0600000US2501330840|archive-url=https://archive.today/20200213235156/https://factfinder.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/ACS/17_5YR/B04004/0600000US2501330840|url-status=dead|archive-date=February 13, 2020|publisher=[[United States Census Bureau]]|access-date=January 13, 2020|title=People Reporting Single Ancestry: 2013-2017 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates - Holyoke city, Hampden County, Massachusetts}}</ref>

===Chinese===
[[File:Holyoke, Mass 141 Laundry Mr Lee Wong Hing.gif|left|thumb|A High Street laundry shop owned and operated by Mr. Lee Wong Hing,{{efn|name="pinyin"|Note all names used in early 20th century Western sources predate [[pinyin]].}} a Chinese American merchant, c. 1904, from a review case by Federal Government, in the era of the [[Chinese Exclusion Act]]]]

{{external media|image1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20200206072133/http://leonardjlosholyokehistory.blogspot.com/2015/10/the-orient-dubbed-holyokes-restaurant.html The Orient Restaurant], c. 1935, it was drafted in 1919 by [[George P. B. Alderman]] under commission by owner Joe Fun{{efn|name="pinyin"}}<ref>{{cite magazine|title=Holyoke, Mass.- Contracts Awarded. Chinese Restaurant.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OS9YAAAAYAAJ&pg=RA6-PA59|volume=XL|magazine=The American Contractor|page=59|date=February 22, 1919|publisher=F. W. Dodge Corp|location=Chicago}}</ref>}}

As of the 2010 Census, there were 79 residents of Chinese heritage living in Holyoke (''Chinese'': 霍利奥克), and an estimated 119 according to the 2017 [[American Community Survey]].<ref name="Race2010"/> [[Chinese Americans]] have resided in small numbers in Holyoke, as well as its neighboring cities of Springfield and Westfield, since the mid 19th century. Though only a demographic of dozens, their early presence represented two classes, a working class operating laundromats and restaurants, and an academic demographic attending Holyoke High School through the [[Chinese Educational Mission]] and similar exchanges from 1872 through 1911;<ref name="Johnson">{{cite book|title=Hampden County, 1636-1936|editor-last=Johnson|editor-first=Clifton|pages=453–454|chapter-url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=wu.89067299784&view=1up&seq=475|oclc=9479870|volume=I|chapter=Chapter XXVIII: Racial Groups in Hampden County|year=1936 |publisher=American Historical Society }}</ref> a number of alumni would become prominent officials, overseeing reforms in the [[Qing dynasty]] and the [[Republic of China (1912–1949)|Republic of China]] thereafter.<ref name="Holyoke Transcript-Telegram">{{cite news|title=Of High Degree; Distinguished Chinese Here, Chow Wan Tang Visits Holyoke After 27 Years Absence|work=Holyoke Transcript-Telegram|date=July 14, 1908|location=Holyoke, Mass.|quote=Two of China's most brilliant and distinguished officials are spending this week in Holyoke as guests in the Kagwin home in Elmwood. They are Chow Wang Tang who is general manager of the Chinese Telephone and Telegraph company and Mr Yun also an official of the same...Mr Wan Tang graduated from the Holyoke high school and left Holyoke 27 years ago...They are now on their way home and leave Holyoke Friday morninf [sic] for San Francisco whence they will sail for China}}</ref><ref name="clarencecuba">{{cite news|title=Holyoke|page=10|work=Springfield Republican|location=Springfield, Mass.|date=June 5, 1919|quote=Clarence Chow, formerly a student in Holyoke and who has been Chinese vice-consul at Havana, Cuba, has been appointed vice-consul for Australia. He arrived in Holyoke to-day for a brief visit with the Kagwin family on the Beech-street extension before proceeding on his way to Australia}}</ref>

In the 1880 US Census, 4 Chinese residents were recorded as residing in the city.<ref>{{cite book|title=Report of the Social Statistics of Cities; Part I. The New England and the Middle States; Part II. The Southern and the Western States|publisher=Government Printing Office|year=1886|location=Washington, D.C.|editor=George E. Waring, Jr.|volume=Part I|page=220|quote=35 people of color; 4 Chinese|chapter=Holyoke; Hampden County, United States}}</ref> In the decade following the [[Chinese Exclusion Act]] of 1882, other families would move to the area and by 1893 a letter to the editor of New York's ''Irish American'' reported the population had grown to 20 people.<ref name="IA">{{cite news|title=The City of Holyoke, Mass. [Letter to the Editor]|date=June 17, 1893|page=1|work=Irish American|location=New York}}</ref> These Chinese would form [[tong (organization)|tong chapters]] and other institutions in time, and integrated early on. Reflecting social attitudes, Holyoke would make national news in 1888 when a Holyoke laundryman, one Sam Kee,{{efn|name="pinyin"}} married a white mill worker, Katie Jones, leaving to be wed in New York.<ref>{{cite news|title=Mismated but Married; A Holyoke Chinese Laundryman Takes a Mill Girl for His Bride|date=December 2, 1888|location=Springfield, Mass.|work=Springfield Republican|page=1|quote=Sam Kee of Holyoke, a Chinese laundryman at the corner of High and Lyman streets, caused a sensation yesterday afternoon by going off with a young white girl named Katie Jones, ostensibly to be married. They took the 2.40 train for New York, and Sam told a hackman at the depot that they were to be maried by a Chinaman at the metropolis. The girl was well dressed and intelligent. She has no friends in Holyoke and very little is known about her.}}
* {{cite news|title=Matrimony Notice- Springfield, Mass. dispatch|location=Silver City, Id.|work=Owyhee Avalanche|page=1|date=December 15, 1888}}</ref>  The history of Holyoke and Springfield's Chinese would largely be male-dominated, due to the immigration restrictions imposed on them, by 1925 there would be a ratio of 5.7 Chinese American men to every 1 woman of Chinese descent in the United States.<ref>{{cite news|title=Chinamen in U. S. in Need of Wives; Only 10,000 Women of Race for 57,000 Males in This Country|work=Arkansas Gazette|page=13|date=September 17, 1925|location=Little Rock, Ark.}}</ref> In a Hampden County history by [[Clifton Johnson (author)|Clifton Johnson]], the earliest Chinese community was described as transitory, which may have been in part a reflection of the Federal government's scrutiny of Chinese merchants before the passage of the [[Chinese Exclusion Repeal Act]].<ref name="Johnson"/><ref>{{cite archive |first= Edsell|last= H|item = Reexamination of Lee Wong Hing following an unfavorable report from the Chinese Inspector |type =Textual record |date = February 11, 1904 |series = Chinese Exclusion Act Case Files, ca. 1892 - ca. 1920|file =Lee Wong Hing, 1904 - 1904 |collection = Record Group 85: Records of the Immigration and Naturalization Service, 1787 - 2004 |repository =National Archives |institution =National Archives and Records Administration|location =Washington, D.C.}}</ref> Despite a presence spanning four decades by that time, it was not until 1921 that the first [[Chinese funeral rituals|Chinese funeral rites]] were recorded in Holyoke by ''[[The Republican (Springfield, Massachusetts)|The Republican]]''.<ref>{{cite news|title=Holyoke|page=14|work=Springfield Republican|date=June 16, 1921|location=Springfield, Mass.|quote=Henry Chong, believed to be the first Chinese resident of Holyoke to die here, passed away today at the Holyoke City hospital. He had been engaged with his brother, Charlie, in the laundry business for several years at 473 High street. He came to Holyoke about 25 years ago. The Chinese funeral customs will be observed.}}</ref> Though not Holyoke specifically, a 1942 account of [[Westfield, Massachusetts|Westfield]]'s last first-generation Chinese laundromat closing would describe that respective towns peak in Chinese laundromats being about 1911 to 1918.<ref>{{cite news|title=Mack Charlie's Departure Closes Era of Chinese Laundries in Westfield|page=42|location=Springfield, Mass.|work=Springfield Republican|last=Guinasso|first=John J.|date=March 22, 1942}}</ref>

Although limited in scale by the lack of a sizable population, Holyoke and Springfield would briefly see the violence of the [[Tong Wars]]. A prolonged rivalry between the [[On Leong Chinese Merchants Association|On Leong]] and [[Hip Sing Association|Hip Sing]] [[Tong (organization)|tongs]], present in Holyoke and Springfield, came to a head on December 7, 1924 when a drive-by shooting injured two members of the On Leong tong at a Springfield laundromat.<ref name="tongwar">{{cite news|page=4|work=Springfield Republican|location=Springfield, Mass.|date=August 7, 1929|title=Tong Outbreaks Recall Shootings Here During 1924; Two On Leong Men Seriously Wounded and Jury Failed to Convict Men Tried for Shooting|quote=The outbreaks between the Hip Sing and On Leong tongs throughout cities of the country recalls the situation in this city [Springfield] in 1924 when two On Leong tongmen were shot. The night of December 7, 1924...Police guarded against reprisals for a long time as the On Leong tong is more powerful than the Hip Sing tong in this city [Springfield].}}</ref> Although no suspect was convicted, Holyoke's Joe Fun, who'd opened  "The Orient" restaurant five year's earlier faced scrutiny as the driver and a reported member of the Hip Sing, barricading himself in his business across from City Hall for days with his lawyers.<ref>{{cite news|title=Chinese Tong Fighters May Be Deported...Investigation in Holyoke|page=1|work=Springfield Republican|location=Springfield, Mass.|date=December 10, 1924|quote=Local [Springfield] and Holyoke police are working on a report from local members of the On Leong tong that Joe Fun, proprietor of a Holyoke Chinese restaurant and reputed leader of the Hip Sing in this locality, drove Albert Foo, alias Eng Foo, and Sing Fun, alias Chang Loo, now under arrest for attempted murder, to Springfield Sunday afternoon, a few hours before the actual shooting took place and stopped in front of 22 Liberty Street, the scene of the gunplay. Edward J. Gould of New York city, member of the law firm of Gould & Gould, counsel for the Hip Sing, was in Holyoke yesterday and in conference with Joe Fun and a private detective. Joe fun is said to have barricaded himself in his restaurant on Dwight street, opposite the Holyoke city hall, since the occurrence in Springfield Sunday night.}}</ref> Later denying his tong membership, Fun approached the Holyoke Police in 1927, seeking protection, and it was reported police were watching a laundromat on Appleton Street at that time, hoping to prevent additional skirmishes.<ref>{{cite news|title=Holyoke Chinese Fear Trouble; Joe Fun, Former Tong Leader Asks Police for Protection After Strange Chinese Arrive in City|location=Springfield, Mass.|page=1|work=Springfield Republican|date=March 27, 1927|quote=Joe Fun, proprietor of the Orient restaurant and former leader of the Hip Sing tong in Holyoke, this morning applied to the police department for protection. The presence in the city of a number of strange Chinese has created a stir in Oriental circles. The Appleton street laundry, the recognized headquarters of On Leong tong in this city is being watched closely}}</ref>

The other class of Chinese residents who resided in Holyoke were the sons of officials in Qing China, of whom about a dozen were accepted from 1872 to 1881 at [[Holyoke High School]], one of numerous other public schools in the Commonwealth to host such students.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://chinacomestomit.org/chinese-educational-mission/|title=Chinese Educational Mission at MIT|publisher=MIT Libraries|year=2017|website=China Comes to MIT|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180614175508/http://chinacomestomit.org/chinese-educational-mission/|archive-date=June 14, 2018}}</ref> The exchange program left such an impression on its alumni, some would return to the city as senior officials of the Qing government. These included a Mr. Shung Kih Ting, who visited to Holyoke in 1909 while acting deputy commissioner of the [[Chinese Maritime Customs Service]],<ref>{{cite news|title=Chinese Official in Holyoke; Brings Young Son and Two Other Chinese Boys to Spend Some Time with Mrs. N. L. Dickerman of Northampton Street|date=May 17, 1904|page=7|work=Springfield Republican|location=Springfield, Mass.}}
</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Class of 1884, Harvard College; Twenty-Fifth Anniversary Report of the Secretary|volume=VII|date=June 1909|chapter=Shung Kih Ting|quote=Immediately on arrival at Springfield, Massachusetts, he and his chum, Wong Liang Tun, went to Holyoke, Massachusetts under the charge of Mrs. H. S. Dickerman. Under the careful direction and instruction of that most worthy lady he was able, in the autumn of 1876, to enter the Holyoke High School, where he completed the four years' course without missing a school day, and graduated third in his class...In January, 1908, he received his present appointment (acting assistant statistical secretary), acting deputy commissioner of customs...}}</ref> and Mr. Chow Wan Tang, then general manager of the [[Imperial Chinese Telegraph Administration]].<ref name="Holyoke Transcript-Telegram"/> Although the Chinese Educational Mission had ended by this time, in 1908 Chow Wan Tang would leave his son, Clarence Chow, to study as he had once, at Holyoke High School.<ref name="yale">{{cite news|title=Holyoke and Grank Trunk|quote=Clarence Chow, son of former Commissioner of Telephone and Telegraph Chow of China, has returned to Yale, where he is a student, after a visit at the Kagwin home on Beech-street extension.|page=19|date=March 3, 1912|work=Springfield Republican|location=Springfield, Mass.}}</ref> Clarence was hosted by the same family who had hosted his father, the Kagwins on Beech Street, a working-class family in the employ of the city's Ford Augur Company. Clarence went on to become an acclaimed school athlete at Holyoke High, before attending Yale.<ref>{{cite news|title=Holyoke's Chinese Athlete; Clarence Chow Generally a Point-Winner in High School Track Games|date=March 26, 1911|page=21|work=Springfield Republican|location=Springfield, Mass.|quote=Clarence Chow, a Chinese boy, is one of the best athletes at the Holyoke high school. This boy is a star performer in the pole vault and in other events he does exceptionally well. In the various indoor and outdoor meets which Holyoke high has competed in for the past two years, Chow has been a consistent point-winner. The boys at the school all feel sure of some points when he is in form. He has had fine success in the indoor meets the past season and the students at Holyoke are banking on him for some points in the outdoor meets this spring.}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Holyoke Social Notes|page=16|work=Springfield Republican|date=July 6, 1919|location=Springfield, Mass.|quote=The friends of Clarence Chow, a former pupil at the high school, who is now on his way to Australia where he is to act as consul for the Chinese government, have been much interested to meet his brother, Fred Chow. The latter entered Cornell university as a freshman last winter and recently visited the Kagwin family where Clarence once made his home.}}
* {{cite news|title=Obituary|quote=Beriah H. Kagwin, 86...|date=September 10, 1915|page=14|location=Springfield, Mass.|work=Springfield Republican}}
* {{cite news|title=Dies Suddenly; D. H. Kagwin Was Expected to Join His Family This Week|page=10|location=Springfield, Mass.|work=Springfield Union|date=July 3, 1912}}</ref> 
<ref name="clarencecuba"/> Returning to China in the years after college, Chow would spend the rest of his time in the service of the Chinese government across three administrations, enduring political turmoil of the [[Chinese Civil War]]. Arriving in Holyoke as a Qing government exchange student, he would serve as a diplomat for the Republic, and later wrote his classmates in 1961, to say that he was serving as a teacher in [[Beijing]] during [[Mao]]'s administration.<ref>{{cite news|title=Reunion Fetes Are Held By Five Alumni Groups|date=May 28, 1961|page=11|location=Springfield, Mass.|work=Springfield Union|quote=John S. Begley was chairman of the program. Among the letters read from class members was one from Clarence Chow, now behind the Communist lines teaching in Peking, China. Chow, a native of China, resided here for many years and during his school days was a popular class member and athlete}}</ref>

Aside from exchange students the city would host one other prominent official. In May 1906, [[Chen Jintao]],{{efn|Referred to by contemporary Western documents in the [[Wade–Giles]] Romanization as "Ch’en Chin-t’ao" or "Chintao Chen".}} the eventual founder of the [[Bank of China]], also regarded as China's first foreign scholar,<ref name=BDRC>Boorman, Howard L., editor, ''[[Biographical Dictionary of Republican China]]'', "Ch’en Chin-t’ao", Columbia University Press, New York, 1967. I:170:173.</ref> was sent to the city on assignment to study its budding paper-making industry and infrastructure, reporting back to the Chinese government after a month of observation. He would be received not only by mill owners but the city government itself, including city engineer James Tighe who would show him the infrastructure of the [[Holyoke Water Works|Holyoke Reservoir System]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Visiting Holyoke Mills; Chintao Chen, Representative of the Chinese Government, Making a Special Study of the Paper Industry of Holyoke|work=Springfield Republican|page=13|date=May 24, 1906|location=Springfield, Mass.}}</ref> Chen, possibly a member of the [[Tongmenghui]],<ref>{{cite journal|journal=[[Journal of Race Development]]|volume=4|issue=1|page=103|title=The Relation of the Returned Students to the Chinese Revolution|last=Tsao|first=Y. S.|quote=Very few students from Europe and America were members of the 'Tung Men Hwei,' [sic] and judging from their actions only Mr. C. T. Wang, Drs. Chen Hui Wang and Chintao Chen from Yale were the only possible ones|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LN2Aa5DnYYYC&pg=PA103|year=1914}}</ref> would go on to serve numerous important roles in both the [[Qing Dynasty|Qing]] and [[Republic of China (1912–1949)|Republic of China]] governments, including Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs for the latter.<ref>{{cite magazine|title=Flood Prevention in China|quote=Dr. Chen Chin-Tao is now on his way to America to represent his country in negotiations [for $20,000,000 of bonds for engineering work to prevent floods in the Huai River Valley]|page=63|volume=2|issue=5|magazine=Santa Fe Trail Magazine|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=apJFAQAAMAAJ&pg=RA3-PA63|date=May 1914}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|journal=American Journal of International Law; Supplement- Official Documents|page=117|title=Exchange of Notes- Memorandum handed by the Japanese Minister to Dr. Chen Chintao, Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs|volume=11|year=1917|publisher=Oxford University Press|location=New York|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=E3YLAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA117}}</ref>

===Colombians===
As of the 2010 Census, there were 202 residents of Colombian heritage living in Holyoke, and an estimated 204 according to the 2017 [[American Community Survey]].<ref name="HispOriginSF1">{{cite web|url=https://factfinder.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/DEC/10_SF1/PCT11/0600000US2501330840|publisher=[[United States Census Bureau]]|access-date=January 13, 2020|title=Hispanic or Latino by Specific Origin: 2010 Census Summary File 1 - Holyoke city, Hampden County, Massachusetts|archive-url=https://archive.today/20200213162059/https://factfinder.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/DEC/10_SF1/PCT11/0600000US2501330840|archive-date=February 13, 2020|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="HispOrigin">{{cite web|url=https://factfinder.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/ACS/17_5YR/B03001/0600000US2501330840|archive-url=https://archive.today/20200214000239/https://factfinder.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/ACS/17_5YR/B03001/0600000US2501330840|url-status=dead|archive-date=February 14, 2020|publisher=[[United States Census Bureau]]|access-date=January 13, 2020|title=Hispanic or Latino Origin by Specific Origin: 2013-2017 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates - Holyoke city, Hampden County, Massachusetts}}</ref> Though not residents of the city, one of the earliest exchanges between Holyoke and Colombian culture came on October 11, 1889, during the first [[Pan-American Conference]], where the officials of 14 Central and South American countries were received in Springfield and subsequently Holyoke, traveling by rail.<ref name="PanAmReception">{{cite news|title=Our Honored Visitors; Delegates of the Americas; Their Handsome Reception Here; What They Saw and How They Saw It|date=October 12, 1889|page=4|work=Springfield Republican|location=Springfield, Mass.|quote=Argentina...Bolivia...Brazil...Chili [sic]...Colombia...Costa Rica...Guatemala...Honduras...Mexico...Nicaragua...Peru...Salvador...Uruguay...Venezuela...}}</ref> Among them was {{ill|Carlos Martínez Silva|es}}, one of the framers of [[Colombia]]'s [[Colombian Constitution of 1886|1886 Constitution]] which established it as the Republic of Colombia.<ref>{{cite news|title=How They Fared at Holyoke; A Look at the Big Dam and a Run Through a Model Paper Mill|quote=Carlos Martinez Silva of the Colombia delegation perhaps enjoyed the trip to Holyoke most, for Manager Curtis secured him a seat on the locomotive, where he could drink in the beautiful scenery to the best advantage. It was the best view of the Connecticut river the party had had, and it was fully appreciated.|date=October 12, 1889|page=4|location=Springfield, Mass.|work=Springfield Republican}}</ref> Nearly a century later, in the late 1960s, many of the earliest Colombian residents would settle in Holyoke, as laborers in the remaining factories during a labor shortage from the [[Vietnam War]].<ref>{{cite AV media | date = 23 July 2015 | time=1:30 |people= Stefany Garcia| title = Columbian Flag Raising | via = Youtube | url = https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2xl_HFPofgo&t=90 | publisher = Holyoke Media}}</ref>

===Dominicans===
As of the 2010 Census, there were 349 residents of Dominican heritage living in Holyoke, and an estimated 5,080 according to the 2017 [[American Community Survey]], comprising the second largest Hispanic or Latino group in the city.<ref name="HispOriginSF1"/><ref name="HispOrigin"/> In the early 1990s, dozens of Dominican families arrived in Holyoke, some following a similar path as Puerto Rican residents, arriving from New York to Springfield, others directly from the [[Dominican Republic]]. Many would open shops such as [[bodega (convenience store)|bodega]]s and salons in the city.<ref name="Sears 2015"/><ref>{{cite news|title=Hispanic business owners thriving in Holyoke|archive-date=September 14, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190914234002/https://www.wwlp.com/news/massachusetts/hispanic-business-owners-thriving-in-holyoke/|url=https://www.wwlp.com/news/massachusetts/hispanic-business-owners-thriving-in-holyoke/|last=Ricci|first=Monica|date=September 5, 2019|work=WWLP 22-News|publisher=Nexstar Broadcasting, Inc.}}</ref>

===English===
{{external media|image1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20200206191115/https://pbs.twimg.com/media/CyCTg2AXgAAv5QJ?format=jpg&name=4096x4096 Farr Alpaca vs. Clan McLaren, Chaloux Cup, Thanksgiving Day c.1910], an example of the soccer club which ultimately led to a professional team, the Falcos, from the collection of Harry Craven at Highland Hardware, via SoccerHistoryUS}}
As of the 2010 5-year [[American Community Survey]], there were 949 residents of English heritage living in Holyoke, and an estimated 305 according to the 2017 American Community Survey, as well as 53 in that survey who identified by the response "British".<ref name="SingleAncestry2010ACS">{{cite web|url=https://factfinder.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/ACS/10_5YR/B04004/0600000US2501330840|archive-url=https://archive.today/20200213234951/https://factfinder.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/ACS/10_5YR/B04004/0600000US2501330840|url-status=dead|archive-date=February 13, 2020|publisher=[[United States Census Bureau]]|access-date=January 13, 2020|title=People Reporting Single Ancestry: 2006-2010 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates - Holyoke city, Hampden County, Massachusetts}}</ref><ref name="SingleAncestry2017ACS"/> Holyoke's English would comprise two groups, American "Yankee English", descendants of the first settlers of [[Massachusetts Bay Colony]] and soldiers of the [[American Revolution]], including early figures like Mayors [[William B. C. Pearsons]], [[Roswell P. Crafts]], and [[William Whiting II|William Whiting]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Crafts |first=William Francis |title=The Crafts Family: A Genealogical and Biographical History |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=M3XCFlk3sVMC&pg=PA448 |location=Northampton, Mass. |publisher=Gazette Printing Company |year=1893 |pages=301, 448–449, 585 |oclc=191111567 }}</ref><ref name="stone">{{Citation |last = Clark |  first = Rusty | title = Holyoke, Massachusetts: Stories Carved in Stone | publisher = Dog Pond Press | location = West Springfield, MA | year = 2004 | isbn= 0-9755362-6-5}}</ref> The latter group would be the later arrivals of Holyoke, including William Skinner of [[William Skinner and Sons|Skinner Silk]], and American impressionist painter [[William Chadwick (painter)|William Chadwick]], both 19th century arrivals of English immigrant families.<ref>{{cite book|title=Scenic Impressions: Southern Interpretations from The Johnson Collection|last1=Pennington|first1=Estill Curtis|last2=Severens|first2=Martha R|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=q8g0CwAAQBAJ&pg=PT198|page=198|year=2015|publisher=University of South Carolina Press|isbn=9781611177176}}</ref> Many of the cities later arrivals would also be hires for the [[Farr Alpaca Company]], of which about half of its initial 200 workers came directly from Canada or England, and was described as "an English mill". It was through the fanfare of these English and Anglo-Canadian arrivals that the city would briefly host one of the pioneer professional American [[soccer]] teams, the [[Holyoke Falcos]].<ref>{{cite journal|last=Bunk|first=Brian D.|title=The Rise and Fall of Professional Soccer in Holyoke, Massachusetts, USA|publisher=Routledge|date=September 2011|volume=XXXI|issue=3|pages=283–306|journal=Sport in History|doi=10.1080/17460263.2011.618697|s2cid=142019417}}</ref>

===French and French-Canadians===
{{main|History of the French in Holyoke}}
As of the 2010 5-year [[American Community Survey]], there were 1,126 residents of French heritage living in Holyoke, 695 residents of French-Canadian heritage, and no residents of Acadian or Cajun heritage. In the 2017 American Community Survey, it was recorded there were 721 residents of French heritage, 712 residents of French-Canadian heritage, and 13 residents of Acadian or Cajun heritage.<ref name="SingleAncestry2010ACS"/><ref name="SingleAncestry2017ACS"/> At the beginning of the 20th century Holyoke was a hub for [[Franco-Americans|Franco-American]] culture, having one of the largest populations of French or French-Canadian foreign nationals, exceeding the populations of [[Chicago]] and [[New Orleans]] in 1913.<ref name="AmLeader">{{cite magazine|magazine=The American Leader|publisher=American Association of Foreign Language Newspapers, Inc.|location=New York|volume=IV|issue=11|date=December 11, 1913|title=French Towns in the United States; A Study of the Relative Strength of the French-Speaking Population in Our Large Cities|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=j8HMDSORztsC&pg=PA672|pages=672–674}}</ref>

===Germans===
{{main|Germans in Holyoke}}
As of the 2010 5-year [[American Community Survey]], there were 578 residents of German heritage living in Holyoke, and in the 2017 American Community Survey, it was recorded there were 276 residents of German heritage.<ref name="SingleAncestry2010ACS"/><ref name="SingleAncestry2017ACS"/> During the 19th century a small German immigrant colony was established around the Germania Woolen Mills of [[South Holyoke]], which had the highest German per capita population of New England by 1875.<ref name="turnenNsport">{{cite book|title=Turnen and Sport|editor=Annette R. Hofmann|chapter=Translating Gymnastics Into Economic and Political Power: The Rise and Decline of the German Turnverein in Holyoke, Massachusetts, 1871–1910|pages=121–146|publisher=Waxmann Münster|location=New York, München, Berlin|year=2004|author=Gerhard Wiesinger}}</ref>

===Greeks===
[[File:Holy Trinity Greek Orthodox Church (Holyoke, Massachusetts 1918).png|thumb|right|The Holy Trinity Greek Church in [[South Holyoke]], as it appeared shortly after its dedication, from the 1918 history book ''Hellenism in America'']]

As of the 2010 5-year [[American Community Survey]], there were 113 residents of Greek heritage living in Holyoke (''Greek'': Χόλιοκ), and an estimated 37 according to the 2017 American Community Survey.<ref name="SingleAncestry2017ACS"/>

Although a large Greek community would characterize Springfield more than Holyoke in size and cultural institutions, at the turn of the 20th century the Paper City would see the arrival of a Greek families seeking work in the area's mills and factories.<ref>{{cite news|title=In and About Springfield; The Greeks of This City; Colony Has Grown Rapidly|page=10|location=Springfield, Mass.|work=Springfield Republican|date=October 13, 1912}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=In and About Springfield; The Greeks of this City; Colony has Grown Rapidly|date=October 13, 1912|page=10|work=Springfield Republican|location=Springfield, Mass.}}</ref> The first arrivals were largely individual workers in the local textile factories, with the first family, that of George Demos, arriving in 1904.<ref name="storyof"/>{{rp|231}} By 1905 there were reportedly 25 Greek expatriates living in the Paper City.<ref name="OrthodoxHistory">{{cite web|last=Vulopas, Th. D.|first=Harry Savas|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190705112925/http://holytrinityholyoke.ma.goarch.org/about_us/history|archive-date=July 5, 2019|url=http://holytrinityholyoke.ma.goarch.org/about_us/history|title=Highlights in the History of the Church of the Holy Trinity|website=Holy Trinity Greek Orthodox Church, Holyoke, MA|publisher=Department of Internet Ministries, Metropolis of Boston}}</ref>

Holyoke's community was largely built around the [[Greek Orthodox|Orthodox]] Church, even prior to the construction of its permanent home. In the earliest years the community was hosted in the grand hall of the [[:File:Monument National Canadien Français, Holyoke, Massachusetts.jpg|Monument National Canadien Français]], at which the first Greek Orthodox church services were held by Reverend Papaleloudas, as well as [[Celebration of the Greek Revolution|celebrations of the Greek Revolution]], and meetings of the Pan-Hellenic Union of America, which had 20,000 members in 1913 and maintained a branch in Holyoke.<ref>{{cite news|title=Greeks Join in a Big Celebration; Meeting in Monument Hall With Addresses in Honor of 98th Anniversary of Independence—Cablegram to Wilson Urging Justice for Greece|date=April 14, 1919|page=9|location=Springfield, Mass.|work=Springfield Republican}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Pan-Hellenic Union Official is Guest; Greeks Enjoy Banquet and Speec by Papamihalopoulos|page=9|work=Springfield Union|location=Springfield, Mass.|date=October 13, 1913}}</ref> During the [[Second Balkan War]] in 1913, the organization would receive letters from those of the community fighting for their country overseas, with at least 40 such men going overseas for the effort against [[Bulgaria]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Many Holyoke Greeks in War; Bulgarian Atrocities Related in Letters Sent to Paper City|date=July 16, 1913|page=13|work=Springfield Union|location=Springfield, Mass.}}</ref>

On May 19, 1916, the Holy Trinity Church was officially issued a charter of parish by the Secretary of the Commonwealth, and the process began in the construction of a permanent church edifice. The parish would hire Greek-American architect Kyriakos Kalfas of New York City, who would base the design on the Church of the Pantokrator in [[Patras]], but decided to use welded steel for the edifice's domes rather than traditional wood and tile-based building methods, seeking to prevent ice and snow from compromising the structure.<ref name="OrthodoxHistory"/> The church was dedicated on November 18, 1917.<ref>{{cite news|title=Byzantine Dedication; Greek Church at Holyoke|date=November 18, 1917|page=5|location=Springfield, Mass.|work=Springfield Republican}}</ref>

By 1920 there were a reported 400 members of the Greek community residing in Holyoke, and although they were united by the Greek Hellenic identity and independence of their nation, rifts existed in the earliest days between those supporting [[Eleftherios Venizelos]] and the [[Monarchy of Greece|Greek monarchy]], with some tensions and confrontations between the two factions at meetings during the early 1920s.<ref name="telegram">{{cite news|title=Greeks Wire President; Deny That They All Favor Prebiscite to Choose Ruler of Greece|work=Springfield Republican|location=Springfield, Mass.|page=14|date=November 10, 1920}}</ref> During one 1920 meeting held at [[Holyoke City Hall|City Hall]], it was reported that the City Marshall (a predecessor of the Chief of Police) withdrew support and suggested the meeting of 1,200 be called off due to reported tensions between the two factions.<ref>{{cite news|title=Holyoke Greeks at Odds; City Marshal Nolen Withdraws Permission for Them to Hold Mass-Meeting|page=11|location=Springfield, Mass.|work=Springfield Republican|date=August 1, 1920}}</ref> Though the meeting was still held with a police presence, a week later one of its speakers, a Greek diplomat, Elias Panas, would be attacked by members of an opposing faction while in Springfield.<ref>{{cite book|title=New York Times Index for the Published News|volume=VIII|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AD9NAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA279|page=288|quote=Panas, Elias—attacked by fellow Greeks at Springfield, Mass. Ag. 8. 22:3|year=1920}}</ref> Later in November of that same year, members of the Venizelos faction, Holyoke's Greek Liberal Society, would telegram [[Woodrow Wilson|President Wilson]], decrying a piece that had been published by a New York paper calling for a new referendum for a ruler of Greece, arguing it was done so by royalists.

By 1920, the Greek language had briefly found a home in the city's press, with the establishment of the New England Greek-American Publishing Company in [[South Holyoke]] at 419 Main Street, by one Christ Bress.<ref>{{cite book|title=N.W. Ayer & Son's American Newspaper Annual and Directory|page=424|year=1922|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qadEAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA424}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Weddings: Angelopoulos—Christopoulos|quote=...in the presence of nearly 200 guests who came from Holyoke, Mass., New York, Danielson[ , Conn.], Newar, N. J., Attleboro and Woburn, Mass...The couple were attended by Christ Bress, editor of the Greek weekly newspaper, The Voice of Greece, of Holyoke, Mass., who was best man|date=May 17, 1920|page=6|location=Norwich, Conn.|work=Norwich Morning Bulletin}}</ref> Mr. Bress would also found the fraternal St. Andrews Club in the city, and later worked as a writer for the first successful [[Greek language]] daily, the ''[[Atlantis (newspaper)|Atlantis]]'' in New York City, shortly before his death in 1929. Unfortunately little information remains on the duration of his paper in Holyoke, other than his involvement in its publication had ceased by that time.<ref>{{cite news|title=Man Killed In Bus Accident Was Former Magazine Editor Christ Bress of New York|work=The Sheboygan Press|location=Sheboygan, Wisc.|date=September 21, 1929|page=6|quote=Man Killed In Bus Accident Was Former Magazine Editor Christ Bress of New York, who was cremated in a Sheboygan-Fond-du Lac motor coach after it crashed with an automobile on County Trunk Z west of Plymouth Monday. [Bress] was a former newspaper and magazine editor and fraternal organization worker, according to information received by The Press from the L. C. Markatos company by whom he was employed as a salesman. He was a graduate of a Greek university and of "the law course at the University of New Mexico", and he taught school in Greece and in the United States. His favorite subjects were history and philosophy. Mr. Bress was at one time editor of a Greek newspaper and up to the time of his death he was a writer of feature articles in the Atlantis, a daily Greek newspaper of New York City. He was at one time president and secretary of the St. Andrew Club of Holyoke, Mass., and was one of the founders of the society.}}</ref>

During the [[Iouliana]] of 1965, through the efforts of the Holy Trinity Greek Church as well as the First Baptist Church and 3 other Baptist congregations, two families were received from Greece to make their new home in Holyoke.<ref>{{cite news|title=Two Greek Families 'Overwhelmed' on Arriving at Holyoke|page=11|work=Springfield Union|location=Springfield, Mass.}}</ref> On March 28, 2022, [[Joshua A. Garcia|Mayor Garcia]] honored the community with a raising of the flag of Greece and official proclamation celebrating [[Greek War of Independence|the independence of Greece]] from the Ottoman Empire in 1821.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.masslive.com/news/2022/03/holyoke-raises-greek-flag-celebrates-history.html|title=Holyoke raises Greek flag, celebrates history|last=Hohenberger|first=Dennis|publisher=MassLive|work=The Republican|location=Springfield, Mass.|date=March 29, 2022}}</ref>

===Irish===
{{main|History of the Irish in Holyoke}}
As of the 2010 5-year [[American Community Survey]], there were 2740 residents of Irish heritage living in Holyoke, and in the 2017 American Community Survey, it was recorded there were 1882 residents of Irish heritage.<ref name="SingleAncestry2010ACS"/><ref name="SingleAncestry2017ACS"/> From the beginning of Holyoke's founding, Irish immigrants have been associated with the founding of the City; prior to its formal establishment the area today encompassing Holyoke, the Third Parish of West Springfield, was known as "Ireland", or "Ireland Parish".<ref name=Holland1855>{{cite book |last=Holland |first=Josiah Gilbert |date=1855 |title=History of Western Massachusetts; the counties of Hampden, Hampshire, Franklin, and Berkshire |url=https://archive.org/stream/historyofwestern02holluoft#page/70/mode/2up |location=Springfield, Mass. |publisher=Samuel Bowles |pages=70 |quote=On the 7th of July, 1786, the part of West Springfield now embraced in Holyoke was incorporated as the Third Parish of West Springfield, and was called 'Ireland', and 'Ireland Parish', from the fact that several Irish families were the first settlers of the territory, though there is no record of the date of their settlement}}</ref>

===Italians===
{{multiple image
   | direction = horizontal
   | width1 = 112
   | width2 = 250
   | align = left
   | footer = Rigali Block at 341-343 High Street; built by fruit store owner Louis Regali in 1887, and designed by [[George P. B. Alderman]], it was later sold to Caesar Equi who operated his store there in the 20th century (''right''). Equi's would be the first such store to operate in the city with its own soda fountain, selling its own ice cream<ref name="storyof"/>
   | image1 = Rigali Block, Holyoke, Massachusetts.jpg
   | image2 = Equi%27s_Store,_Holyoke,_Massachusetts_circa_1910.jpg}}
As of the 2010 5-year [[American Community Survey]], there were 565 residents of Italian heritage living in Holyoke, and an estimated 320 according to the 2017 American Community Survey.<ref name="SingleAncestry2017ACS"/> Italians, having a greater presence toward Springfield, would arrive in Holyoke in the 1880s, with the earliest record of an Italian family being in 1884 when a Charles Marano married a May O'Connor. Many of the city's earliest arrivals would establish confectionery stores and produce markets in business districts along High and Main Streets.<ref name="PVpict">{{cite book|title=Pioneer Valley: A Pictorial History|last=McLain|first=Guy A|publisher=The Donning Company|location=Virginia Beach, Va.|year=1991}}</ref>{{rp|95}} In addition to proprietors, many of these early arrivals included tradesmen such as stone-cutters, carpenters, tailors, and barbers. By 1887, one Louis J. Rigali, a real estate broker, would construct a small Romanesque block on High Street, still extant today.<ref name="storyof"/>{{rp|164–167}}

While the Italian community would remain scattered throughout the city, for a brief time a section of downtown by present-day Nick Cosmos Way (then known as "Bond Street") would be characterized by a number of Italian shops and family residences, with the first market dedicated to Italian specialties like olive oil, cheeses, and cold-cuts, opening at the corner of Bond and Essex in 1918. A number of other markets and produce stores founded by Italian immigrants would remain fixtures for more than 50 years, including names like Luchini's, Rigali Brothers, Mazzolini Brothers, and Magri's, the latter of which remains extant in Chicopee. Another example of a long-running Holyoke Italian business was D'Addario's Camera Shop, operated by brothers Vincent and [[Ray D'Addario]], the latter of whom would go on to be chief photographer of the [[Nuremberg trials]].<ref name="storyof"/>{{rp|164–167}} One of the longest-running Italian institutions in the city would be the Italian Progressive Society. Founded in 1900, as a [[benefit society]], the group would host numerous dances, dinners, and outings, buying a plot of land adjacent to [[Hampton Ponds State Park|Hampton Ponds]]. Similar to the German Turners' Camp Jahn, the Italian Grove would serve as a family recreation venue for membership in the summers. In 1972 the Society reorganized, incorporated again in South Hadley in 1978, and gradually became defunct by the 21st century.<ref>{{cite news|title=Italian Society Plans Ball|work=Springfield Union|date=October 5, 1975|page=49|location=Springfield, Mass.}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Italian Club to Mark 50th Anniversary; Progressive Society Plans Joint Observance Columbus Day|page=9|location=Springfield, Mass.|work=Springfield Union|date=September 22, 1951}}</ref>

===Mexicans===
As of the 2010 Census, there were 167 residents of Mexican heritage living in Holyoke, and an estimated 329 according to the 2017 [[American Community Survey]].<ref name="HispOriginSF1"/><ref name="HispOrigin"/> While much of Holyoke's Mexican community arrived in the latter part of the 20th and early 21st centuries, the city had some earlier exchanges of Mexican culture. In the late 1890s, one of the musical acts performing at [[Mountain Park (Holyoke, Massachusetts)|Mountain Park]] were the Mexican Troubadours, a group of musicians from [[Mexico]] wearing traditional [[Charro outfit|charros]], who would play the harp, [[ocarina]], mandolin, and "a sort of exaggerated [[autoharp]]" there,<ref>{{cite news|title=["The Mexican troubadours..."]|date=December 14, 1897|page=4|work=Springfield Republican|location=Springfield, Mass.|quote=The Mexican troubadours are exponents of the harp, mandolin, ocarina and a sort of exaggerated autoharp, with all of which instruments they make very sweet music.}}</ref> as well as regularly at Springfield's [[Forest Park, Springfield, Massachusetts|Forest Park]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Society and Personal Mention|quote=The Mexican troubadours, musicians of Mexico, playing the native instruments and dressed in the national costume, will be at Grant's restaurants in Forest park this week, playing afternoons in Woodside lodge and evenings in Waldesruhe|date=May 24, 1896|location=Springfield, Mass.|work=Springfield Republican|page=8}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=For A New Library at Holyoke|quote=The Mexican Troubadours will be at Mountain park to-morrow and Monday|date=May 31, 1896|page=6|location=Springfield, Mass.|work=Springfield Republican}}</ref> The Mexican government would also send delegations to Holyoke on two occasions. In 1889, during the cross-country tour of the [[Pan-American Conference]], when the city received Adolfo Mujica y Sáyago, a diplomat who would later serve as the Consul General of Mexico to Spain.<ref name="PanAmReception"/><ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=El Mundo Illustrado|volume=XI|issue=2|language=es|title=Necrologia- El Sr. Cónsul de México en España|page=3|date=October 30, 1904|location=Puebla de Zaragoza, Mex.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VeMxAQAAMAAJ&pg=PT502}}</ref> In 1950, representatives from Mexico, among more than a dozen other countries, were on-hand during the demonstration of the first newsprint commercially produced using [[bagasse]] at the mills of the Chemical Paper Company.<ref>{{cite news|title=Paper Making from Cane Waste to Get First Practical Test Today—Representatives of 15 Countries to Witness Printing Demonstration at Holyoke, Mass.—Subsidiary Developing Group Formed|department=Business & Finance Section|page=20|date=January 28, 1950|work=The New York Times|via=United States Congress House Committee on the Judiciary, Subcommittee No. 5|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0GRFAQAAMAAJ&pg=RA3-PA1197}}</ref>

===Polish===
{{multiple image
   | direction = horizontal
   | width1 = 280
   | width2 = 150
   | align = right
   | footer = [[Mater Dolorosa Parish, Holyoke|Mater Dolorosa Parish]] (''lower-right''), [[Pulaski Park (Holyoke, Massachusetts)|Pulaski Park]] (''left''), and the old Polish Ward One neighborhood in 1937, prior to its redevelopment in the late 20th century; a 1942 [[Holyoke Gas & Electric]] ad for [[Mazda (light bulb)|Mazda lamps]] in Polish, from ''[[Gwiazda (Holyoke)|Gwiazda]]'', ''[[Gwiazda (Holyoke)|The Polish Weekly Star]]''
   | image1 = Pulaski Park and old Ward 1 of Holyoke, Massachusetts during Flood of 1936.jpg
   | image2 = Holyoke Gas & Electric, Polish Advertisement (from Gwiazda, 1942-08-29).png}}

As of the 2010 5-year [[American Community Survey]], there were 1,705 residents of Polish heritage living in Holyoke, and an estimated 1,307 according to the 2017 American Community Survey, making them the fourth largest group by single responses.<ref name="SingleAncestry2017ACS"/>

The first [[Polish people|Polish]] would settle in Holyoke in the mid-to-late 1880s, having arrived in [[Chicopee, Massachusetts|Chicopee]] in 1880 and [[Northampton, Massachusetts|Northampton]] in 1886.<ref name="STCCpolish">{{cite web|title=Polish Immigrants in the Valley|website=Our Plural History - Springfield, MA|archive-date=May 19, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170519082559/http://ourpluralhistory.stcc.edu/industrial/polish.html|url=http://ourpluralhistory.stcc.edu/industrial/polish.html|year=2009|publisher=Springfield Technical Community College}}</ref> One of Holyoke's earliest Polish settlers was Joseph Czarnecki, who arrived in September 1888. By 1895, the community had grown to 300 residents, many of whom were working as textile makers in [[Lyman Mills (company)|Lyman Mills]].<ref name="storyof"/>{{rp|123,126}}
<ref name="CatholicHistory">{{cite book|title=History of the Catholic Church in the New England States|editor1-last=Byrne|editor1-first=William|editor2-last=Leahy|editor2-first=William A.|editor3-last=McCoy|editor3-first=J. J.|editor4-last=O'Donnell|editor4-first=Jasiel H.|editor5-last=Dowling|editor5-first=A.|editor6-last=Finen|editor6-first=John E.|editor7-last=Young|editor7-first=Edmund J. A.|editor8-last=Michaud|editor8-first=John S.|volume=II|publisher=The Hurd & Everts Co.|location=Boston|year=1899|last=McCoy|first=John J.|chapter=Church of the Poles—Mater Dolorosa. Holyoke.|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gJlQAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA680|pages=680–681}}</ref> Because of their profession and class, this group largely lived near the French-Canadians near the north end of Downtown by Ward 4, in the Lyman Mills Housing by Oliver Street, as well as in parts of [[The Flats, Holyoke, Massachusetts|The Flats]].<ref>{{cite news|title=The Pure Blood of France– Our French-Canadian People; Their History and Traits|work=Springfield Republican|pages=11–12|location=Springfield, Mass.|date=December 11, 1904}}</ref><ref name="AmericanizationNYTrib"/> In the earliest days of their arrival, the Holyoke's Poles held a tense, skeptical attitude toward city police, for as one ''[[Springfield Republican]]'' journalist put it— "nothing is so much feared in the Polish settlement as a police officer and in this the people show the result of years of government under a military system," the aforementioned system reflecting the realities of a [[History of Poland (1795–1918)|Partitioned Poland]].<ref>{{cite news|title=About Affairs at Holyoke|date=July 28, 1895|page=4|location=Springfield, Mass.|work=Springfield Republican}}</ref>

With the growth of the community, many sought to establish a Catholic church in the city which would offer [[Mass (liturgy)|mass]] in the [[Polish language]]. However the [[Roman Catholic Diocese of Springfield in Massachusetts|Diocese of Springfield]] did not move to establish such a parish until Rev. A. N. Dynia, a priest from Poland who had been defrocked, had begun to organize such a church there himself.<ref name="CatholicHistory"/><ref>{{cite news|title=Catholic Notes|work=St. Albans Daily Messenger|date=April 24, 1896|page=3|quote=An edict was issued recently by Bishop Beaven, of Springfield, forbidding the Polish Catholics of Holyoke, under penalty of excommunication, from attending a church recently established in holyoke by Rev. A. N. Dynia, a Polish priest who has been wandering about from place to place in the western part of this country. He came to Holyoke recently and immediately prepared to build a small church and found a parish among the Polanders of that city. He claimed to be working under the direction of Bishop Beaven, and succeeded in securing an attendance of over 100 of his countrymen, most of them from that part of their native country from which he claimed to have come. A priest coming from Poland must have a document from the propaganda at Rome to certify that he is qualified and to prove that his record is clear. Rev. A. N. Dynia has no such testimonials, and consequently has not been allowed to carry on the work of an ordained priest. The Polish residents of Holyoke have, therefore, been under the guidance of Rev. H. Chalupka, of Chicopee, and special service for them have been held in the Church of the Holy Rosary every Sunday. The project of establishing a church of Polish Catholics in Holyoke has often been proposed, but until the priest who has been causing the trouble came to Holyoke, the plan was not put into execution|location=St. Albans, Vt.}}</ref> Indeed the independent Dynia would continue this pattern going westward, similarly unofficially initiating the creation of other Polish parishes as he went from town to town, only to be shunned by each respective Diocese.<ref>{{cite book|title=The History of the Diocese of Columbus: The History of fifty years, 1868-1918|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_HpQAQAAMAAJ|year=1918|publisher=Diocese of Columbus|page=402|quote=Rev. A. Dynia came and immediately began to build a structure...Rev. A. Dynia stayed but a short time...}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=A History of the Poles in America to 1908: The Poles in Illinois|volume=II|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bOF1AAAAMAAJ|page=256|publisher=Catholic University of America Press|year=1994|isbn=9780813208091}}</ref><ref name="polishofficial">{{cite news|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200201035946/https://www.masslive.com/news/2017/05/polish_official_tells_bishop_h.html|archive-date=February 1, 2020|url=https://www.masslive.com/news/2017/05/polish_official_tells_bishop_h.html|date=January 7, 2019|title=Polish official tells bishop he supports sale of Mater Dolorosa Church in Holyoke|last=Plaisance|first=Mike|work=The Republican|location=Springfield, Mass.}}</ref> After Dynia was "driven from the city", the Bishop appointed Father H. Chalupka of Chicopee to attend to this would-be parish, and on September 26, 1896, Rev. Anthony M. Sikorski became the first resident priest.<ref name="CatholicHistory"/> In 1901 a building designed by Holyoke's [[George P. B.
