Alderman]] was built and paid for by the parishioners who sold it to the Diocese at a token price, by 1902 the ''[[New York Tribune]]'' identified their community synonymous with [[Mater Dolorosa Parish, Holyoke|Mater Dolorosa]].<ref name="polishofficial"/> An influential member of the Polish community in the early 20th century was John Zielinski, who first arrived in Holyoke in 1912 to serve as the organist and choir director of Mater Dolorosa and was subsequently vice-president of the [[Polish Roman Catholic Union of America]] at one time, instrumental in the work of adjusting to American culture while keeping traditions of the Old World.<ref name="storyof"/>{{rp|123,126}}<ref>{{cite book|volume=VIII|title=Encyclopedia of Massachusetts|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uEIDAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA266|pages=265–266|publisher=The American Historical Society|location=New York|year=1916}}</ref><ref name="MD">{{cite book|last=Osgood|first=Gilbert C.|url=https://archive.org/details/storyofholyokech00osgo/page/6|pages=6–7|year=1890|location=Holyoke, Mass.|publisher=Transcript Publishing Company|title=Story of the Holyoke Churches}}</ref>

Gradually the community established itself in Ward 4 in the land immediately adjacent to this church. In 1923 one Stanislaw Walczak established a Polish-language weekly, the ''Gwiazda'' or ''The Polish Weekly-"Star"'' which would carry local news as well as syndicated national news, ultimately folding after 3 decades, in 1953.<ref>{{cite web|publisher=Library of Congress|website=Library of Congress Online Catalog|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200201053242/https://www.loc.gov/item/sn86071595/|archive-date=February 1, 2020|url=https://www.loc.gov/item/sn86071595/|title=Gwiazda = Polish weekly-star}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=[Colophon]|url=https://archive.org/details/GwiazdaHolyokeMass.August291942/page/n1/mode/2up|work=Gwiazda|location=Holyoke, Mass.|publisher=Stanislaw Walczak|volume=XIX|issue=35|date=August 29, 1942}}</ref> Similarly to the French ''[[La Justice]]'', the Polish press continued as a private printer run by the same family, even decades after the paper had ceased publication. The Star Press, as it was later known, remained extant as recently as 2004 with one of its last regular jobs being the publication of the first issue of  ''[[El Sol Latino]]''.<ref>{{cite news|work=El Sol Latino|location=Amherst|url=https://issuu.com/elsollatino/docs/el_sol_latino_jan2018_web|date=January 2018|title=The importance of being a Puerto Rican Newspaper|quote=In November 2017, ''El Sol Latino'' celebrated its 13 anniversary. Since our first edition, published in the now-defunct Star Press of Holyoke...}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|website=USAOpps|url=https://www.usaopps.com/government_contractors/contractor-5541419-STAR-PRESS-INCORPORATED.htm|title=Star Press Incorporated|quote=Contract Person: John Walczak|access-date=February 1, 2020}}</ref>
{{external media|audio1=[https://archive.org/details/78_south-street-polka_larry-chesky-and-his-orch-t-krosinowski_gbia0529252b ''South Street Polka''], 1954, by [[Larry Chesky]], named for the thoroughfare of [[Elmwood, Holyoke, Massachusetts|Elmwood]]}}
Polka music would remain popular in Holyoke, as well as neighboring towns and cities in the Pioneer Valley, throughout the 20th century. One of the notable acts of the Paper City being [[Larry Chesky]] and his orchestra, a regular at [[Mountain Park (Holyoke, Massachusetts)|Mountain Park]] for decades, and a later inductee into Chicago's [[International Polka Association|International Polka Hall of Fame]] for his development and promotion of the "Big Band" or "East Coast" style of polka, with more than 100 albums of various artists in the genre featured on his [[Rex Records (1957)|Rex Records]] label, as well as over 100 albums on his and other labels himself.<ref>{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200201054955/https://www.discogs.com/label/129098-Rex-Records-5?page=1&genre=All&limit=500|archive-date=February 1, 2020|url=https://www.discogs.com/label/129098-Rex-Records-5?page=1&genre=All&limit=500|title=Rex Records (5)|website=Discogs}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=International Polka Association Editorial Staff|title=Larry Chesky – Living Category – Inducted 1985|url=http://www.ipapolkas.com/blog/otw-portfolio/larry-chesky-living-category-inducted-1985/|website=International Polka Association|access-date=2014-09-22|archive-date=2016-03-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303234748/http://www.ipapolkas.com/blog/otw-portfolio/larry-chesky-living-category-inducted-1985/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

The Polish community would also see representation in politics at a municipal and state level, with one of the Holyoke Polish community to serve longest in state office being Stephen T. Chmura, an alderman for ward 4, a Massachusetts delegate to the [[1960 Democratic National Convention]], and state representative for Holyoke's respective district in [[Hampden County, Massachusetts|Hampden County]] from 1951 through 1968.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/publicofficersof19671968bost/page/118/|title=Public officers of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts|year=1968|page=119|publisher=Massachusetts General Court}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://politicalgraveyard.com/bio/chipp-chmielewski.html#448.11.29|website=The Political Graveyard|title=Chipp to Chmura}}</ref> Similarly [[Evelyn Chesky]] would get her start in politics as a member of the Holyoke city council, later serving as state representative for the 5th Hampden District.<ref>{{cite book|page=99|url=https://archive.org/stream/publicofficersof19992000bost#page/98/mode/2up|publisher=Massachusetts General Court|title=1999-2000 Public Officers of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts}}</ref>

In recognition of the predominantly Polish neighborhood, in 1939 Prospect Park was renamed [[Pulaski Park (Holyoke, Massachusetts)|Pulaski Park]] for [[Casimir Pulaski]] the Patriot-supporting Polish commander in American Revolution. By the end of the 20th century, one of the city's Polish-American sons, historian [[Edward Pinkowski]] would rediscover Pulaski's burial site in [[Savannah, Georgia]].<ref>{{cite book|page=221|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BwoRAQAAMAAJ|last=Kajencki|first=Francis C.|year=2001|publisher=Southwest Polonia Press|title=Casimir Pulaski, Cavalry Commander of the American Revolution|isbn=9780962719059 }}</ref> With deindustrialization however and the upward mobility of many in the community, the neighborhood would gradually see a decline as more joined communities in Granby, Hadley, and Northampton, and large swathes of land in that section of High Street would be razed in the late 1960s.<ref name="storyof"/>{{rp|123}}<ref>{{cite thesis|title=Cohesion and disintegration in the Polish community of Ward Four, Holyoke, Massachusetts|last=Savage|first=Linda E.|publisher=Mount Holyoke College|year=1967|oclc=978276107}}</ref> In the 1970s the activism of residents and a local friar led to some urban renewal projects, including the "Pulaski Heights" senior citizen housing.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FATiAAAAMAAJ|title=A History of the American Province of Saint Anthony of Padua of the Order of Friars Minor Conventual, 1906-1982|last=Haas|first=Rger M.|year=1982|publisher=St. Anthony of Padua Province|page=84|quote=Stimulated by this friar, the city of Holyoke itself entered the story of Mater Dolorosa and began a reconstruction of this part of the city. Old buildings were torn down. A modern highrise apartment for Senior Citizens, called "Pulaski Heights,"}}</ref> One of the final vestiges of the former community, the Mater Dolorosa Church, was abruptly closed in 2011 when the Diocese stated its steeple was at risk of imminent collapse.<ref>{{cite news|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160327081855/https://www.masslive.com/news/index.ssf/2011/10/judge_rules_mater_dolorosa_pro.html|url=https://www.masslive.com/news/index.ssf/2011/10/judge_rules_mater_dolorosa_pro.html|archive-date=March 27, 2016|title=Judge rules Mater Dolorosa protesters can stay in Holyoke church for now|last=DeForge|first=Jeanette|publisher=MassLive|work=The Republican|location=Springfield, Mass.|date=October 28, 2011}}</ref> Despite sit-in protests, an effort to create a historic district recognizing the area's ties to the city and Pioneer Valley's Polish community, and a proposal deal to sell the church to the city, with the Diocese retaining control of its artifacts and use, the church was ultimately demolished in December 2018, its steeple being the final piece to be razed.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.wggb.com/2013/10/03/holyoke-residents-look-to-create-a-polish-heritage-district/ |title=Holyoke Residents look to create a Polish Heritage District - Western Massachusetts Breaking News and First Warning Weather with WGGB.com ABC 40 |access-date=2013-11-19 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131007235104/http://www.wggb.com/2013/10/03/holyoke-residents-look-to-create-a-polish-heritage-district/ |archive-date=2013-10-07 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181223163843/https://www.masslive.com/news/index.ssf/2018/06/mater_dolorosa_church_purchase.html|url=https://www.masslive.com/news/index.ssf/2018/06/mater_dolorosa_church_purchase.html|archive-date=December 23, 2018|title=Holyoke Council rejects purchase of Mater Dolorosa Church|last=Plaisance|first=Mike|work=The Republican|location=Springfield, Mass.|date=June 28, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Demolition underway at former Mater Dolorosa Church in Holyoke|last1=Trowbridge|last2=Keane|first1=Ryan|first2=Amanda|publisher=Western Mass News|url=https://www.westernmassnews.com/news/demolition-underway-at-former-mater-dolorosa-church-in-holyoke/article_13f5546a-fd6e-11e8-a370-3b1b36f31b8d.html|date=December 11, 2018}}</ref> Although much of the brick and mortar is gone, today a Polish community remains extant in Holyoke and the Greater Springfield area; much of its history and artifacts may be found at the Polish Center of Discovery and Learning in neighboring Chicopee.

===Puerto Ricans===
{{main|Puerto Ricans in Holyoke}}
As of the 2010 US Census, there were 17,825 residents of [[Puerto Ricans|Puerto Rican]] heritage living in Holyoke, and an estimated 18,557 according to the 2017 American Community Survey, making them the largest group by single response ancestry.<ref name="HispOriginSF1"/><ref name="HispOrigin"/> In the 2010 Census, Holyoke had the largest Puerto Rican population, per capita, of any city in the United States outside [[Puerto Rico]] proper, with 44.7% of residents being of Puerto Rican heritage, comprising 92.4% of all [[Latinos]] in the community.<ref name="USCensus">{{cite web|url=http://factfinder.census.gov/faces/tableservices/jsf/pages/productview.xhtml?pid=DEC_10_DP_DPDP1 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20200212055711/http://factfinder.census.gov/faces/tableservices/jsf/pages/productview.xhtml?pid=DEC_10_DP_DPDP1 |url-status=dead |archive-date=February 12, 2020 |title=2010 Census American FactFinder |access-date=August 30, 2013}}</ref>

===Scottish===
{{see also|Holyoke Caledonian Pipe Band|Caledonia Building}}
[[File:Holyoke_Caledonian_Benefit_Club.svg|thumb|left|150px|Emblem of the former Holyoke Caledonian Benefit Club]]
[[File:Holyoke_Caledonian_Pipe_Band_performing_in_the_2019_Holyoke_Saint_Patrick's_Day_Parade.jpg|thumb|right|The [[Holyoke Caledonian Pipe Band]] in the 2019 Holyoke Saint Patrick's Parade; established in 1910, it is the oldest continuously operating [[pipe band]] in the United States<ref name="highlandgames"/><ref>{{cite book|title=Warrior Dreams: Playing Scotsmen in Mainland Europe|page=87|publisher=Manchester University Press|last=Hesse|first=David|year=2014|isbn=9781847799173|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=G4s8CwAAQBAJ&pg=PA87}}</ref>]]
As of the 2010 5-year [[American Community Survey]], there were 208 residents of Scottish heritage living in Holyoke, and an estimated 55 according to the 2017 American Community Survey, as well as 61 in that survey who identified by the response "[[Scotch-Irish Americans|Scotch-Irish]]" and 53 who responded "British".<ref name="SingleAncestry2010ACS"/><ref name="SingleAncestry2017ACS"/>

Holyoke's earliest Scottish settlers would arrive soon after its foundation. Around 1853 the Glasgow Mill at the foot of the [[Hadley Falls Dam]] recruited 82 unmarried women from its namesake city, while Lyman Mills recruited 151 that same year<ref>{{cite book|last=Herman|first=Arthur|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3e9DAT257LkC&pg=PA395|page=395|quote=The confidence in Scottish workers extended to women workers. In 1853 an agent for Hadley Falls Mills in Massachusetts recruited eighty-two unmarried women mill workers from Glasgow, while one in Holyoke in Holyoke Mills hired sixty-seven. In a couple months they had earned enough to pay off their entire transatlantic fare and buy themselves some new clothes and shoes|title=How the Scots Invented the Modern World: The True Story of How Western Europe's Poorest Nation Created Our World & Everything in It|publisher=Three Rivers Press|location=New York|year=2001|isbn=9780307420954}}</ref> Turnover would be extraordinarily high in these mills, as they were with other groups initially imported as workers, with nearly 4 out of 5 of these women leaving within three years.<ref>{{cite journal|volume=XXVIII|issue=1|title=Labor in a Massachusetts Cotton Mill, 1853-60|last=Ginger|first=Ray|date=March 1954|pages=67–91|journal=The Business History Review|jstor=3111446|doi=10.2307/3111446|s2cid=154694256}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Employing Bureaucracy|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xCt6AgAAQBAJ&pg=PA26|page=26|last=Jacoby|first=Sanford M.|publisher=Lawrence Erlbaum Associates Publishers|location=Mahwah, N. J.|year=2004|isbn = 9781135705480}}</ref>

Gradually more Scottish families came to area initially through these mills, generally finding other work in the years thereafter. In 1879, a representative of the [[Order of Scottish Clans]] was received by the local community at a reception in the Hotel Hamilton. However the group, not feeling the organization was acted in their interest, ultimately decided to set up a [[benefit society]] of their own, and on November 22, 1879, the Holyoke Caledonian Benefit Society was organized with a charter member of 21. By its 25th anniversary in 1904 this number had grown to 225, and 450 members by the 50th anniversary of 1929. Originally set up as a sickness and disability insurance fund, the benefit society would also promote Scottish literature, poetry, and music, with such gatherings as celebrations of the life and poetry of [[Robert Burns]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Clans Gather in Honor of Burns; Holyoke Scotch Residents Celebrate Birthday with Concert, Ball and Banquet. Speeches on Poet's Life|date=January 27, 1913|page=10|work=Springfield Union|location=Springfield, Mass.}}</ref> Defunct before 1962,<ref>{{cite news|title=Alexander MacDonald|date=February 19, 1962|page=5|work=Springfield Union|location=Springfield, Mass.|quote=He was a member of...the former Holyoke Caledonian Benefit Club Inc.}}</ref> the Caledonian Society's most enduring namesake, the [[Holyoke Caledonian Pipe Band]], established in 1910, is today the longest continuously active [[pipe band]] in the United States.<ref name="highlandgames">{{cite book|title=The Scottish Highland Games in America|last=Donaldson|first=Emily|page=110|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oorzjF7ZTzIC&pg=PA110|year=1998|publisher=Pelican Publishing Company|isbn=9781455611713}}</ref> Its legacy also endures today in its former banquet hall, the historical [[Caledonia Building]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Golden Jubilee of Caledonians at Holyoke 23D; 50th Anniversary of Organization Will Be Celebrated—History and Growth of Organization|page=9|location=Springfield, Mass.|work=Springfield Republican|date=November 3, 1929}}</ref> A separate entity from the Caledonians, in 1905, the grand conference for the grand women's auxiliary of [[Scottish clans]] was held in the city, being the first time such a gathering was held in any city other than Boston.<ref>{{cite news|title=Scottish Clans Gather; Sixth Annual Convention of the Grand Auxiliary Held Here|date=February 23, 1905|page=4|work=Springfield Republican|location=Springfield, Mass.}}</ref>

Holyoke was also for several decades the hometown of Scottish-born noted golf course architect [[Donald Ross (golfer)|Donald Ross]], who was first brought to the city in 1912 to aid with the design of the Mount Tom Golf Club by [[Joseph L. Wyckoff]], for whom the course is today known as the Wyckoff Country Club. Wyckoff, a member of the executive committee of the Massachusetts Golf Association, would become one of Ross's early patrons, providing him with the financial backing to dedicate more of his time to golf course design rather than serving as a golf pro as he had been partially up until that time.<ref>[https://mhc-macris.net/details?mhcid=hly.1343 HLY.1343], Massachusetts Cultural Resource Information System (MACRIS)</ref><ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=The American Golfer|title=Mt. Tom Golf Club|volume=XIII|page=136|year=1914|quote=President Wyckoff remarked that the club and the city of Holyoke are to be congratulated in that Donald Ross, the links expert, has made his permanent home in Holyoke, the club, particularly, in having Mr. Ross as chairman of its green committee}}</ref><ref name="wyckoffross">{{cite news|title=Donald Ross the 'King Pin' of American Golf|date=December 26, 1919|page=12|last=Paton|first=Larry|work=Boston Herald}}</ref> In 1921 more than 300 Holyoke residents, Mayor Cronin, the Holyoke Police, and members of Mount Holyoke, International, and Smith College would also receive visited by Colonel Walter Scott (1861–1935), a philanthropist who took great interest in the support of scholarships, Scotch educational and cultural initiatives, police work, and a host of other charitable causes.<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=The Caledonian|location=New York|date=December 1921|publisher=Caledonian Publishing Company|title=Rare Day for Walter Scott|pages=415–416|volume=XXI|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Hzw-AQAAMAAJ&pg=PA416}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|website=PoliceHistory.com|title=Colonel Walter Scott|archive-date=July 11, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190711133500/http://www.policehistory.com/wsbiog.html|url=http://www.policehistory.com/wsbiog.html|quote=He endowed medals for bravery by policemen in New York, Boston, Worchester, Holyoke, Detroit, in Argentina and, of course, in Ireland.}}</ref>

===Native Americans===
Before the arrival of Europeans, Algonguin tribes such as Pequots, Mohegans, and Chippewas inhabited the area.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.holyoke.org/history-of-holyoke/#:~:text=The%20first%20inhabitants%20of%20Holyoke,Pequots%2C%20Mohegans%2C%20and%20Chippewas.|title=History of Holyoke}}</ref>

==Religion==
===Christian===
{{multiple image
   | direction = horizontal
   | width1 = 264
   | width2 = 145
   | width3 = 193
   | width4 = 138
   | width5 = 147
   | align = center
   | footer = (''Left to right''): Examples of Holyoke churches, the Sacred Heart Church (Our Lady of Guadeloupe), the Catholic parish which gave the [[Churchill, Holyoke, Massachusetts|Churchill]] neighborhood its namesake; the Second Baptist Church, used by other Evangelical groups, presently vacant; St. Patrick's Chapel of St. Jerome's Parish; the First Lutheran Church, identified by its preceding building as the German Lutheran Church; United Congregational Church of Holyoke, before the addition of Skinner Chapel, formerly known as Second Congregational Church
   | image1 = Sacred Heart Church in 19th century, Holyoke, Massachusetts.png
   | image2 = Second Baptist Church Holyoke.JPG
   | image3 = Saint Patrick Chapel, Saint Jerome Church, Holyoke, Massachusetts.JPG
   | image4 = First Lutheran Church (Holyoke, Massachusetts).JPG
   | image5 = Exterieur van de Second Congregational Church te Holyoke Second Cong. Church (titel op object), RP-F-2001-7-1059-13.jpg
}}
Holyoke is home to houses of worship for numerous denominations of Christianity and Judaism. One of the city's oldest monikers was [[Elmwood, Holyoke, Massachusetts|Baptist Village]] as the first congregation established there was the First Baptist Church of Holyoke, which first erected a meetinghouse in 1792, traces its origins to five baptisms on the shores of the Connecticut in 1725, and continues as a congregation today.<ref name="stone"/>

As of 2010 an estimated 60% of Holyoke is religious, with the largest demographic being Christians, more specifically [[Roman Catholic]]s, who comprise 49% of the city's population.<ref name="bestplaces.net">[https://www.bestplaces.net/religion/zip-code/massachusetts/holyoke/01040 Holyoke, Massachusetts Religious Statistics], Sperling's BestPlaces.</ref> In 2011, two Catholic parishes, [[Holy Cross Parish, Holyoke|Holy Cross]] and [[Mater Dolorosa Parish, Holyoke|Mater Dolorosa]] were merged into Our Lady of the Cross Parish.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ourladyofthecross.com/about-us|title=About Us|publisher=Diocese of Springfield, Massachusetts|access-date=2020-02-06|archive-date=2018-03-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180307023146/http://ourladyofthecross.com/about-us|url-status=dead}}</ref> A number of other Catholic parishes, including Our Lady of Guadalupe, St. Jerome's, and Immaculate Conception Parish also reside in the city.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20180304134531/http://www.parishesonline.com/find/st-jerome-parish-1040 St. Jerome Parish, Holyoke], ParishesOnline</ref><ref>[http://icholyoke.com/index.html Immaculate Conception Parish] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200206064028/http://icholyoke.com/index.html |date=2020-02-06 }}, Holyoke</ref>

In addition to its parishes, the city has a number of convents of [[Nun#Distinction between a nun and a religious sister|sisters]] including the [[Sisters of Providence of Holyoke]] in [[Ingleside, Holyoke, Massachusetts|Ingleside]], the [[Sisters of St. Joseph#Sisters of St. Joseph of Springfield (Massachusetts)|Sisters of St. Joseph of Springfield]] who maintain group homes there, and the [[Sisters of St. Francis of Assisi]] in [[Highland Park, Holyoke, Massachusetts|Highland Park]].

[[Protestantism|Protestant]] congregations have played a significant role in Holyoke's civic life since its founding, including the First Congregational Church of Holyoke, founded in 1850,<ref>[http://www.uccholyoke.org United Church of Christ of Holyoke], Holyoke, Massachusetts</ref> the First Lutheran Church of Holyoke, founded in 1867,<ref>[https://www.lutheranholyoke.org/ First Lutheran Church of Holyoke]</ref> and the United Methodist Church of Holyoke, South Hadley, and Granby, which meets in [[South Hadley, Massachusetts|South Hadley]], which was founded in 1810.<ref>[thesteepleinthefalls.org The Steeple in the Falls], United Methodist Church of Holyoke, South Hadley, and Granby</ref>

A [[Greek Orthodox]] church, Holy Trinity Greek Orthodox Church, has also existed in the city since its founding in 1917.<ref>[http://www.holytrinityholyoke.ma.goarch.org/ Holy Trinity Greek Orthodox Church], Metropolis of Boston</ref>

===Jewish===
[[File:Holyoke Rodphey Shalom Park St Synagogue.png|right|thumb|Perspective sketch of an early synagogue building in South Holyoke, designed for Congregation Rodphey Shalom by George P. B. Alderman in 1903]]
{{external media|image1=[https://archive.org/details/JewishHistoryExhibitFor75thAnniversaryOfHolyoke Jewish History Exhibit For 75th Anniversary Of Holyoke (1948)], taken from ''[[Holyoke Transcript-Telegram]]'' negative|float=left}}
Holyoke is also home to a significant Jewish population. As one of 35 municipalities in Massachusetts with more than 100 Jewish residents, Holyoke is home to an estimated 1,300 residents observing the faith and two synagogues, Congregation Sons of Zion, a [[Reform Judaism|Reform]] congregation, and Congregation Rodphey Sholom, practicing [[Orthodox Judaism|Orthodoxy]].<ref name="jvlibrary">{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170218150908/http://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/massachusetts-jewish-history|archive-date=February 18, 2017|publisher=American Israeli Cooperative Enterprise|website=The Jewish Virtual Library|title=Massachusetts, United States|url=http://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/massachusetts-jewish-history}}</ref>

The 1890 Census described 5 Jewish families, of German origin, however in the city's earliest decades they were largely unrepresented by any synagogue or association.<ref name="harperjewish">{{cite book | last1=Harper | first1=Wyatt E. | title=The Story of Holyoke | year=1973 | publisher=Centennial Committee of the City of Holyoke |chapter=Jewish Immigration To Holyoke|chapter-url=https://archive.org/stream/storyofholyoke00harp/#page/170|page=170| oclc=8060402 |url = https://archive.org/stream/storyofholyoke00harp#page/n0/mode/2up}}</ref> Though statistics remain unknown, anecdotally some had turned to [[Crypto-Judaism]] or abandoned their faith altogether, to better assimilate with the local population.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Secret Jews of Holyoke: the Davis Family|archive-date=May 16, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180516170439/https://sarahglucksterngenealogy.wordpress.com/the-oconnor-wood-families/the-secret-jews-of-holyoke-the-davis-family/|url=https://sarahglucksterngenealogy.wordpress.com/the-oconnor-wood-families/the-secret-jews-of-holyoke-the-davis-family/|last=Gluckstern|first=Sarah|website=Sarah G's Genealogy|year=2014}}</ref> By 1916 a [[gemach]] was established in the city, the Hebrew Free Loan Society of Holyoke, and by 1918 an estimated 1,000 Jews resided in the Paper City.<ref>{{cite web|website=Scripophily|archive-date=November 26, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161126133046/https://scripophily.net/hebfreloanso.html|url=https://scripophily.net/hebfreloanso.html|title=Hebrew Free Loan Society of Holyoke - Massachusetts}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=American Jewish Yearbook|year=1921|page=373|url=http://hillel.org/docs/default-source/historical/american-jewish-year-book-(1920-1921).pdf?sfvrsn=2|via=Hillel.org|access-date=2020-07-19|archive-date=2020-11-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201111235949/https://hillel.org/docs/default-source/historical/american-jewish-year-book-%281920-1921%29.pdf?sfvrsn=2|url-status=dead}}</ref> Though the earliest of these Jewish arrivals were a handful of [[Ashkenazi]] from Germany who arrived with the Germania Mills immigrant colony, later arrivals would also hail from [[Russia]] as its territory is known today, as well as from [[Vilnius]] of modern-day [[Lithuania]].<ref name="harperjewish"/><ref>{{cite book|title=Men of New England|publisher=American Historical Company|location=New York|url=https://archive.org/details/menofnewenglandc01unse|year=1941|chapter=William Paul Yoerg; Executive and Civic Leader|pages=54–55|chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/menofnewenglandc01unse/page/62}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Hampden County, 1636-1936 - Individual and Family Records|editor-last=Johnson|editor-first=Clifton|page=68|chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/hampdencounty16303john/page/510/mode/2up|volume=III|chapter=Max Aaron Jacobson|year=1936 |publisher=New York, The American historical Society }}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=The National Cyclopædia of American Biography|page=191|publisher=[[James Terry White|James T. White & Company]]|location=Clifton, N. J.|quote=BAROWSKY, Jacob Louis, business executive, was born in Vilna, Russia...as cochairman of the Connecticut-Western Massachusetts region of NCCJ [National Conference for Christians and Jews]|editor1=George Derby|oclc=60498648}}</ref>

By 1946 there were about 475 Jewish families residing in Holyoke;<ref>{{cite web|url=https://archive.org/details/JewishHistoryExhibitFor75thAnniversaryOfHolyoke|title=Jewish History Exhibit for 75th Anniversary of Holyoke|publisher=Holyoke Transcript-Telegram|date=1948}}</ref> reflecting this growth, as well as the suburbanization of subsequent generations of Holyoke Jews, both the [[Reform Judaism|Reform]] and [[Orthodox Judaism|Orthodox]] synagogues would see new buildings constructed in the following decade with Sons of Zion, the former, breaking ground in 1949, and Rodphey Sholem, the latter, moving from its [[South Holyoke]] to Northampton Street in 1953.<ref name="harperjewish"/><ref>{{cite news|title=Carry Torahs Into Rodphey Sholem Synagog|date=September 2, 1953|location=Springfield, Mass.|page=9|work=Springfield Union}}</ref>

From the earliest decades of the 20th century, Jewish members of the community saw the support of a wide swath of Holyoke's civic society. It was around the turn of the century that the two extant Jewish congregations were formally established. Congregation Sons of Zion, a [[Reform Judaism|Reform]] congregation, and Congregation Rodphey Sholom, practicing [[Jewish Orthodoxy|Orthodoxy]]. Both originated at the end of the 19th century, with Rodphey Sholom founded in 1903 but tracing its heritage to the Paper City Lodge of the Order Brith Abraham, founded in 1899, and Sons of Zion being founded in 1901. Today both congregations hold joint services during certain holidays.<ref name="harperjewish"/><ref>{{cite news|title=Sons of Zion Celebrates 110 Years|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170604213443/http://www.wmassjewishledger.com/2014/03/sons-of-zion-celebrates-11o-years/|archive-date=June 4, 2017|date=March 2014|url=http://www.wmassjewishledger.com/2014/03/sons-of-zion-celebrates-11o-years/|work=The Western Mass. Jewish Ledger|location=Springfield, Mass.}}</ref><ref name="jvlibrary"/>
During the [[Pogroms in the Russian Empire|Russian pogroms]] of the early 1900s, one such event was an interfaith call to worship, with [[Nathan P. Avery|Mayor Avery]] and clergy of several churches rendering speeches at the Rodphey Sholem Synagogue in [[South Holyoke]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Stirring Words at Holyoke; Hebrew Mass-Meeting of Protest Draws Strong Speeches From the Mayor, City Solicitor and Several Clergymen|date=November 20, 1905|work=Springfield Republican|location=Springfield, Mass.|page=4}}</ref> In Holyoke's history a number of Jewish entrepreneurs and civic leaders would shape the city, including [[Clemens Herschel]] who would develop his modern [[Venturi meter]] for the [[Holyoke Water Power Company]] in the 1880s,<ref>{{cite book|author=Madison Clinton Peters|title=The Jews in America; A Short Story of their Part in the Building of the Republic|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hWJ2AAAAMAAJ&pg=PA90|page=90|quote=Clemens Herschel is a recognized authority on hydraulic engineering|publisher=The John C. Winston Company|location=Philadelphia|year=1905}}</ref> and Jacob Barowsky who would develop and market [[Lestoil]] in the early 20th century. In its history the city has had two Jewish [[List of mayors of Holyoke, Massachusetts|mayors]], the first, [[Samuel Resnic]],<ref>{{cite news|last=Feinberg|first=Mark|title=Holyoke's Mayor-Elect Created 500 Jobs in City|newspaper=The Boston Globe|date=November 10, 1957}}</ref> elected in 1957, and the second, [[Alex Morse]], elected in 2012.

===Other===
As of 2020, [[Sperling's BestPlaces]] estimated 0.6% of the population of Holyoke adhered to another religion, including 0.2% observing some form of [[Islam]], and 0.4% observing unnamed [[Eastern religions]].<ref name="bestplaces.net"/> Among the Eastern religions observed, a small [[Sikh]] community is extant in Holyoke, and in April 2019 was recognized by the city government in a raising of the Sikh National Flag outside [[Holyoke City Hall|City Hall]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Holyoke honors Sikh community with City Hall flag raising, call to prevent violence|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190415013910/https://www.masslive.com/news/2019/04/holyoke-honors-sikh-community-with-city-hall-flag-raising-calls-to-prevent-violence.html|archive-date=April 15, 2019|url=https://www.masslive.com/news/2019/04/holyoke-honors-sikh-community-with-city-hall-flag-raising-calls-to-prevent-violence.html|last=Hohenberger|first=Dennis|work=The Republican/MassLive|location=Springfield, Mass.}}</ref>
